blocks.text: PUBLIC ADMINISTRATION
SEMESTER V & VI
SHORT NOTES & LONG NOTES
For use by students of Govt. T. Romana College only.

International organisation means organised cooperation among states through permanent institutions. Its evolution before and up to the First World War reflected growing need for cooperation beyond national boundaries.

International organisations are formal institutions with permanent structures, created by agreement among states (intergovernmental organisations) to pursue common objectives. Before the First World War, several forms developed: (1) diplomatic conferences and the Concert of Europe (after the Congress of Vienna, 1815), in which great powers met to manage European affairs; (2) international river commissions - the Central Commission for the Navigation of the Rhine (1815) and the European Commission of the Danube (1856); (3) 'public international unions' for technical cooperation - the International Telegraph Union (1865, now the International Telecommunication Union), the Universal Postal Union (1874), the International Bureau of Weights and Measures (1875), the International Union for the Protection of Industrial Property (1883) and the International Institute of Agriculture (1905, Rome); and (4) the Hague Peace Conferences (1899 and 1907), which adopted conventions on the laws of war and created the Permanent Court of Arbitration (1899).

Non-governmental bodies also developed, such as the International Committee of the Red Cross (1863) and the Inter-Parliamentary Union (1889). These developments reflected the growth of trade, communication and technology, and the need to manage common problems. The devastation of the First World War showed the need for a general political organisation to prevent war, leading to the League of Nations.

The League of Nations was created after the First World War to promote peace and cooperation. Its structure included an Assembly, Council and Secretariat. It achieved some success in cooperation but failed to prevent major aggression and another world war.

The League of Nations was created by the Covenant of the League (26 articles), part of the Treaty of Versailles (1919), largely due to US President Woodrow Wilson's Fourteen Points. It came into existence on 10 January 1920, with headquarters in Geneva. There were 42 founding members; membership reached a maximum of 58. India was a founding member (as part of the British Empire). Organs: the Assembly (all members, one vote each, met annually), the Council (permanent members - Britain, France, Italy and Japan, later Germany and the USSR - and non-permanent members), the Secretariat (headed by a Secretary-General; the first was Sir Eric Drummond) and the Permanent Court of International Justice (The Hague, 1922). Associated bodies included the ILO, the Health Organisation, the Mandates Commission and committees on refugees (the Nansen passport), opium and slavery.

Achievements: settled some disputes (the Aaland Islands between Finland and Sweden, 1921; the Greece-Bulgaria border, 1925), helped refugees and prisoners of war, fought epidemics, regulated drugs, supervised mandated territories and promoted labour standards. Failures: the USA never joined (the Senate rejected the Treaty); Germany (1926-1933) and the USSR (1934-1939) were members only for short periods; Japan (1933), Germany (1933) and Italy (1937) left; decisions required unanimity; it had no armed force; sanctions were weak; and it failed to stop Japan's invasion of Manchuria (1931), Italy's invasion of Ethiopia (1935-1936), German rearmament and expansion, and the outbreak of the Second World War. It was formally dissolved in April 1946, and its assets were transferred to the UN.
The United Nations emerged during the Second World War and was formally established in 1945 as a new international organisation for peace, security and cooperation.

Wartime steps: the London Declaration (June 1941); the Atlantic Charter (August 1941) by Roosevelt and Churchill; the Declaration by United Nations (1 January 1942), signed by 26 nations (the term was coined by Roosevelt); the Moscow Declaration (October 1943) of the USA, UK, USSR and China, calling for a general international organisation; the Tehran Conference (1943); the Dumbarton Oaks Conference (August-October 1944), which drafted proposals; and the Yalta Conference (February 1945), which agreed on the Security Council voting formula (veto).

The United Nations Conference on International Organization at San Francisco (25 April to 26 June 1945), attended by representatives of 50 countries, drafted and signed the Charter on 26 June 1945. Poland signed later, becoming the 51st original member. The UN came into existence on 24 October 1945 (UN Day), after ratification by the five permanent members and a majority of signatories. Its headquarters is in New York. Membership has grown to 193 states (South Sudan, 2011), with observer states such as the Holy See and Palestine.

The UN seeks to maintain international peace and security, develop friendly relations, promote international cooperation and support human rights. Its members are expected to follow the principles laid down in the Charter.

Purposes (Article 1): (1) to maintain international peace and security through collective measures and peaceful settlement of disputes; (2) to develop friendly relations among nations based on equal rights and self-determination of peoples; (3) to achieve international cooperation in solving economic, social, cultural and humanitarian problems and in promoting human rights and fundamental freedoms for all without distinction as to race, sex, language or religion; and (4) to be a centre for harmonising the actions of nations.

Principles (Article 2): sovereign equality of members; fulfilment in good faith of Charter obligations; peaceful settlement of disputes; refraining from the threat or use of force against the territorial integrity or political independence of any state; assistance to the UN in its actions and no assistance to states against which it takes action; ensuring that non-members act in accordance with these principles as necessary for peace; and non-intervention in matters essentially within domestic jurisdiction (except for enforcement measures under Chapter VII).
The UN Charter is the founding legal document of the United Nations. It sets out the purposes, principles, organs and basic rules of the organisation.

The Charter has a Preamble ('We the peoples of the United Nations determined to save succeeding generations from the scourge of war...') and 111 articles in 19 chapters, covering purposes and principles (I), membership (II), organs (III), the General Assembly (IV), the Security Council (V), pacific settlement of disputes (VI), action with respect to threats to peace and acts of aggression (VII), regional arrangements (VIII), international economic and social cooperation (IX), ECOSOC (X), non-self-governing territories (XI), the trusteeship system (XII-XIII), the International Court of Justice (XIV), the Secretariat (XV), miscellaneous provisions (XVI-XVII), amendments (XVIII) and ratification (XIX). The Statute of the ICJ is annexed.

The Charter is a multilateral treaty binding on members; under Article 103, Charter obligations prevail over other agreements. Amendments (Article 108) require a two-thirds vote of the General Assembly and ratification by two-thirds of members, including all five permanent members of the Security Council. Amendments have enlarged the Security Council (from 11 to 15, in 1965) and ECOSOC (from 18 to 27 in 1965 and to 54 in 1973).
The Secretary-General is the chief administrative officer of the UN and performs administrative, diplomatic and political functions under the Charter.

The Secretary-General is appointed by the General Assembly on the recommendation of the Security Council (Article 97), for a five-year term (by practice), renewable once. Selection is subject to the veto of permanent members; regional rotation is followed informally. Since 2016, the process has become more transparent, with public nomination of candidates and informal dialogues. Secretaries-General: Trygve Lie (Norway, 1946-1952), Dag Hammarskjöld (Sweden, 1953-1961), U Thant (Burma, 1961-1971), Kurt Waldheim (Austria, 1972-1981), Javier Pérez de Cuéllar (Peru, 1982-1991), Boutros Boutros-Ghali (Egypt, 1992-1996), Kofi Annan (Ghana, 1997-2006), Ban Ki-moon (South Korea, 2007-2016) and António Guterres (Portugal, 2017-2026). The selection of the next Secretary-General for 2027 is under way.

Functions: (1) administrative - chief administrative officer of the UN; heads the Secretariat; appoints staff; prepares the budget; (2) executive - performs functions entrusted by other organs; (3) political - may bring to the attention of the Security Council any matter that threatens peace and security (Article 99); (4) diplomatic - uses 'good offices' and mediation in disputes (Hammarskjöld's 'preventive diplomacy', U Thant's role in the Cuban Missile Crisis); (5) submits an annual report on the work of the organisation; and (6) acts as the spokesperson of the international community. Trygve Lie called the post 'the most impossible job on this earth'.
The General Assembly is the main deliberative body in which all UN member states are represented. It discusses international issues and makes recommendations within its competence.

The General Assembly (Articles 9-22) consists of all 193 member states, each with one vote. It holds a regular session each year starting in September (the 'general debate' with heads of state and government), special sessions and emergency special sessions. It elects a President for each session. Decisions on important questions (peace and security, election of members of councils, admission of new members, budget) require a two-thirds majority of members present and voting; others need a simple majority. It works through six main committees (disarmament, economic and financial, social and humanitarian, special political and decolonisation, administrative and budgetary, and legal).

Functions: discussing and recommending on any matter within the Charter (except when the Security Council is dealing with it - Article 12); considering principles of cooperation in peace and security, including disarmament; initiating studies and recommendations to promote international cooperation and the development of international law (the International Law Commission, 1947); approving the budget and apportioning expenses among members; electing non-permanent members of the Security Council, members of ECOSOC and (with the Security Council) ICJ judges; appointing the Secretary-General; admitting, suspending and expelling members on the Security Council's recommendation; and receiving reports. Under the 'Uniting for Peace' resolution (1950), it can recommend collective measures when the Security Council fails due to the veto. Its resolutions are generally recommendations, not binding.
The Security Council has primary responsibility for international peace and security. Its structure includes permanent and non-permanent members.

The Security Council (Articles 23-32) has 15 members: five permanent members (China, France, Russia, the UK and the USA) and ten non-permanent members elected for two-year terms by the General Assembly according to equitable geographical distribution (five from Africa and Asia-Pacific, one from Eastern Europe, two from Latin America and the Caribbean, and two from Western Europe and others). India has served eight terms as a non-permanent member (most recently in 2021-2022). The presidency rotates monthly in English alphabetical order.

Voting (Article 27): each member has one vote; procedural decisions need nine votes; substantive decisions need nine votes including the concurring votes of all permanent members (the veto; abstention is not treated as a veto). Powers and functions: primary responsibility for international peace and security (Article 24), with decisions binding on all members (Article 25); investigating disputes and recommending peaceful settlement (Chapter VI); determining threats to peace and taking enforcement measures - sanctions (Article 41) and military action (Article 42) (Chapter VII); establishing peacekeeping operations and sanctions committees; recommending admission of new members and the appointment of the Secretary-General; and electing ICJ judges with the General Assembly. Debates on reform concern expansion of permanent and non-permanent membership and the veto.
The Economic and Social Council coordinates and promotes international economic, social and related cooperation.

ECOSOC (Articles 61-72) has 54 members elected by the General Assembly for three-year overlapping terms, with seats allocated to regional groups. It meets in sessions throughout the year, including the High-Level Political Forum on Sustainable Development (which reviews progress on the Sustainable Development Goals) and the Development Cooperation Forum.

Functions: conducting studies and making reports and recommendations on international economic, social, cultural, educational, health and related matters; promoting respect for human rights; preparing draft conventions; calling international conferences; coordinating the work of specialised agencies through agreements and consultations (Articles 57, 63); and consulting with NGOs (about 6,000 NGOs have consultative status). Subsidiary bodies include functional commissions (Commission on the Status of Women, Commission for Social Development, Statistical Commission, Commission on Narcotic Drugs) and five regional commissions (such as ESCAP in Bangkok, which covers India). Critics say ECOSOC has limited influence compared with the IMF, World Bank, WTO and G20.
The Secretariat carries out the day-to-day administrative work of the UN under the Secretary-General.

The Secretariat (Articles 97-101) comprises the Secretary-General and international civil servants (about 37,000 staff at headquarters in New York and offices in Geneva, Vienna, Nairobi and elsewhere, plus field missions). Staff are recruited on the basis of efficiency, competence and integrity, with due regard to wide geographical representation (Article 101). They must be independent and not seek or receive instructions from any government, and member states must respect their international character (Article 100) - this principle of an independent international civil service is a key feature of international administration.

Departments include the Department of Political and Peacebuilding Affairs, the Department of Peace Operations, the Department of Economic and Social Affairs, the Office for the Coordination of Humanitarian Affairs, the Office of Legal Affairs and the Department of Management Strategy, Policy and Compliance. Functions: administering programmes and policies; preparing studies and reports; servicing meetings; translating documents into the six official languages (Arabic, Chinese, English, French, Russian and Spanish); managing peacekeeping operations; mediating disputes; and informing the public. Reforms have aimed at greater efficiency, accountability, gender parity and decentralisation of management.
The International Court of Justice is the principal judicial organ of the UN and decides legal disputes submitted by states and gives advisory opinions.

The ICJ (Chapter XIV and the Statute of the ICJ) sits at the Peace Palace in The Hague. It replaced the Permanent Court of International Justice of the League. It has 15 judges elected for nine-year terms by absolute majorities in both the General Assembly and the Security Council; one-third are elected every three years; no two judges may be nationals of the same state; and the judges should represent the main forms of civilisation and legal systems. Indian judges have included Sir B. N. Rau, Nagendra Singh (President, 1985-1988), R. S. Pathak and Dalveer Bhandari.

Jurisdiction: (1) contentious cases - only states can be parties; jurisdiction depends on the consent of states, given through special agreements, compromissory clauses in treaties, or declarations accepting compulsory jurisdiction (Article 36(2), the 'optional clause'); judgements are binding and final, and non-compliance may be referred to the Security Council (Article 94); and (2) advisory opinions on legal questions requested by the General Assembly, Security Council and authorised agencies. Sources of law (Article 38): international conventions, international custom, general principles of law, and judicial decisions and teachings of qualified jurists as subsidiary means. India's cases include the Kulbhushan Jadhav case (2019). Limitations: consent-based jurisdiction and lack of enforcement.
The International Labour Organisation promotes labour standards, decent work and social justice through international cooperation.

The International Labour Organization was created in 1919 by Part XIII of the Treaty of Versailles, became the first specialised agency of the UN in 1946, and is headquartered in Geneva. Its unique tripartite structure gives an equal voice to governments, employers and workers. Organs: the International Labour Conference (annual, each member sends two government delegates, one employers' delegate and one workers' delegate), the Governing Body (executive council) and the International Labour Office (secretariat, headed by the Director-General). The Declaration of Philadelphia (1944) stated that 'labour is not a commodity' and 'poverty anywhere constitutes a danger to prosperity everywhere'. It won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1969. India is a founding member and a permanent member of the Governing Body as a country of chief industrial importance.

Functions: setting international labour standards through conventions and recommendations (about 190 conventions); supervising their application through reports and complaint procedures; technical cooperation; research and statistics; promoting the Decent Work Agenda (employment, rights at work, social protection and social dialogue); and the 1998 Declaration on Fundamental Principles and Rights at Work (freedom of association and collective bargaining, elimination of forced labour, abolition of child labour, elimination of discrimination, and since 2022, a safe and healthy working environment). India has ratified six of the eight core conventions originally listed (not the conventions on freedom of association and collective bargaining, Nos. 87 and 98).
The World Health Organisation is the UN specialised agency concerned with international public health.

The World Health Organization was established on 7 April 1948 (World Health Day), headquartered in Geneva. Its governing body is the World Health Assembly of all member states, which meets annually; the Executive Board implements decisions; and the Secretariat is headed by the Director-General (Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus since 2017). It has six regional offices, including the South-East Asia Regional Office in New Delhi. Its constitution defines health as 'a state of complete physical, mental and social well-being and not merely the absence of disease or infirmity'.

Functions: directing and coordinating international health work; setting norms and standards (International Classification of Diseases, Essential Medicines List, vaccine prequalification); supporting countries' health systems; responding to epidemics and emergencies under the International Health Regulations (2005); research; and campaigns against diseases. Achievements: the eradication of smallpox (declared in 1980), the Global Polio Eradication Initiative (India was declared polio-free in 2014), the Framework Convention on Tobacco Control (2003), and coordination of the COVID-19 response and COVAX. Criticisms: slow responses in some emergencies, dependence on voluntary funding from a few donors, and political pressure. The World Health Assembly adopted a Pandemic Agreement in 2025.
The Food and Agriculture Organisation works on food, agriculture, nutrition and related development issues.

The Food and Agriculture Organization was founded on 16 October 1945 (World Food Day) in Quebec City, Canada; its headquarters is in Rome. It has about 195 members (194 countries and the European Union). Its motto is 'Fiat panis' ('Let there be bread'). Organs: the Conference (all members, every two years), the Council and the Director-General.

Functions: fighting hunger, food insecurity and malnutrition; improving agricultural productivity and sustainable agriculture, forestry and fisheries; collecting and analysing data on food and agriculture (FAOSTAT, 'The State of Food Security and Nutrition in the World' report with other agencies); technical assistance to developing countries; early warning of food crises and pests (desert locusts); setting food standards jointly with WHO (the Codex Alimentarius Commission, 1963); and promoting rural development and climate-resilient agriculture. The World Food Programme (WFP, 1961), which provides food aid and won the Nobel Peace Prize in 2020, was created jointly by the UN and FAO. India celebrated the International Year of Millets (2023), proposed by India and declared by the UN General Assembly with FAO's involvement.
The United Nations Development Programme supports development efforts, capacity building and poverty reduction in countries.

The United Nations Development Programme was created in 1965 by merging the Expanded Programme of Technical Assistance (1949) and the UN Special Fund (1958). Headquartered in New York, it works in about 170 countries and territories, funded by voluntary contributions. Its Administrator is one of the most senior UN officials, and it coordinates the UN development system's work at the country level through Resident Coordinators (a role made independent in 2019).

Functions: supporting poverty reduction, sustainable development, democratic governance, peacebuilding, climate and disaster resilience, and capacity-building; helping countries achieve the Sustainable Development Goals (2015-2030); and publishing the Human Development Report (since 1990) with the Human Development Index (life expectancy, education and income), developed by Mahbub ul Haq and Amartya Sen. Other indices include the Gender Development Index, Gender Inequality Index and the Multidimensional Poverty Index. In India, UNDP works with central and state governments on governance, livelihoods, environment, and disaster management (including in the Northeast).

sections.title: International Organisations and League of Nations

blocks.text:
International administration grew from the need for organised cooperation among states. Before and around the First World War, international bodies gradually developed to deal with problems that could not be handled effectively by individual states alone.

The League of Nations was established after the First World War with the objective of maintaining peace through collective cooperation. It had an Assembly, Council and Secretariat and made contributions in several areas of international cooperation. However, weaknesses in membership, enforcement and collective security, along with the aggressive policies of major powers, contributed to its failure to prevent the Second World War.

Evolution of international organisations: the need for cooperation grew with trade, communication and wars; the Concert of Europe (1815) managed great-power relations through conferences; international river commissions (Rhine 1815, Danube 1856) and public international unions (ITU 1865, UPU 1874) handled technical cooperation; the Hague Conferences (1899, 1907) and the Permanent Court of Arbitration promoted peaceful settlement of disputes; NGOs like the Red Cross (1863) developed humanitarian work. These experiences showed the value of permanent secretariats and technical cooperation (David Mitrany's functionalism).

League of Nations: created by the Covenant (1919) as part of the Treaty of Versailles; organs - Assembly, Council, Secretariat, Permanent Court of International Justice; associated bodies - ILO, Health Organisation, Mandates Commission. Principles - collective security (Article 10 and Article 16 sanctions), disarmament, arbitration and open diplomacy. Achievements: settlement of minor disputes, humanitarian work (refugees, health, drugs, slavery), the mandate system and the development of an international civil service. Failures: absence of the USA, withdrawals and expulsions of major powers, unanimity rule, lack of armed forces, weak sanctions, failure in Manchuria and Ethiopia, inability to prevent German aggression and the Second World War.

Lessons: the League's experience shaped the UN - including universal membership, a stronger Security Council with binding powers and great-power participation (veto), specialised agencies for economic and social cooperation, and the International Court of Justice. The League thus represents the first experiment in general international administration.

sections.title: United Nations: Origin, Purposes, Principles and Charter

blocks.text:
The United Nations emerged from wartime cooperation during the Second World War and was established in 1945. It was designed to create a stronger system of international peace and cooperation than the League of Nations.

Its major purposes include maintaining international peace and security, developing friendly relations among nations, promoting cooperation and encouraging respect for human rights. The UN Charter is its foundational legal document and defines the powers and responsibilities of its principal organs.

The Secretary-General is the chief administrative officer and also performs important diplomatic and political roles.

Origin: the Atlantic Charter (1941), the Declaration by United Nations (1942), the Moscow Declaration (1943), Dumbarton Oaks (1944), Yalta (1945) and the San Francisco Conference (April-June 1945), where 50 nations signed the Charter on 26 June 1945. The UN came into existence on 24 October 1945. It was designed to be stronger than the League, with broader membership, a Security Council with binding powers, the veto to keep great powers involved, and an extensive economic and social system.

Purposes and principles: peace and security, friendly relations based on equal rights and self-determination, international cooperation in economic, social, cultural and humanitarian matters and human rights, and harmonising actions of nations; principles of sovereign equality, good faith, peaceful settlement, non-use of force, assistance to UN action and non-intervention. The Charter: Preamble and 111 articles; binding treaty; Article 103 supremacy; amendment procedure; establishes six principal organs (General Assembly, Security Council, ECOSOC, Trusteeship Council - suspended since 1994, ICJ and Secretariat).

Secretary-General: the chief administrative officer and the symbol of the UN; appointed by the General Assembly on the Security Council's recommendation; administrative, executive, political (Article 99) and diplomatic functions ('good offices'); the role has expanded through the leadership of figures like Dag Hammarskjöld (preventive diplomacy, peacekeeping in Suez and Congo) and Kofi Annan (Millennium Development Goals, Responsibility to Protect). The office faces pressure from powerful states and limited resources.

sections.title: Principal Organs of the United Nations

blocks.text:
The General Assembly is the broad deliberative body representing all member states. The Security Council carries primary responsibility for international peace and security. ECOSOC coordinates international economic and social cooperation.

The Secretariat performs the continuing administrative work of the organisation under the Secretary-General. The International Court of Justice is the principal judicial organ and settles legal disputes submitted by states and gives advisory opinions.

These organs divide the political, administrative, economic and judicial responsibilities of the UN.

General Assembly: all 193 members with equal votes; deliberative and recommendatory powers; budget; elections to other organs; admission of members; Uniting for Peace (1950); important declarations (UDHR 1948, decolonisation 1960, SDGs 2015). Security Council: 15 members (P5 with veto, ten elected); primary responsibility for peace and security; binding decisions; peaceful settlement (Chapter VI) and enforcement (Chapter VII); peacekeeping and sanctions. ECOSOC: 54 members; coordinates economic and social work, specialised agencies, functional and regional commissions and NGO consultation; High-Level Political Forum on SDGs.

Secretariat: international civil service under the Secretary-General; administers programmes, peacekeeping, humanitarian coordination, research and conferences; independence of staff (Article 100). International Court of Justice: 15 judges; contentious (consent-based, binding) and advisory jurisdiction; applies international law. Trusteeship Council: supervised trust territories until 1994 (Palau was the last).

Division of responsibilities: the UN's organs divide political (General Assembly and Security Council), economic and social (ECOSOC), administrative (Secretariat) and judicial (ICJ) functions, resembling a separation of powers in international administration. Their effectiveness depends on cooperation among member states, especially the great powers. Problems include the veto, financial constraints, bureaucracy and demands for reform.

The ILO promotes labour rights and social justice. WHO coordinates international health cooperation. FAO deals with food, agriculture and nutrition. UNDP supports development, capacity-building and poverty reduction.

These bodies demonstrate that international administration extends beyond peace and security. It also includes social welfare, health, labour, food security and economic development.

Specialised agencies are autonomous organisations linked to the UN through agreements with ECOSOC (Articles 57 and 63), with their own constitutions, members, budgets and governing bodies. The ILO (1919/1946, Geneva) promotes labour standards, decent work and social justice through tripartite cooperation. The WHO (1948, Geneva) coordinates international health, sets standards, fights diseases and responds to pandemics. The FAO (1945, Rome) works to end hunger, improve agriculture, forestry and fisheries, and provides data and technical assistance.

Funds and programmes (created by the General Assembly and funded voluntarily) include UNDP (1965, New York) for development and the Human Development Report, UNICEF (children), UNEP (environment), UNFPA (population), WFP (food aid) and UNHCR (refugees). Other specialised agencies include UNESCO, the World Bank Group, the IMF, ITU, UPU, ICAO, IMO, WMO, WIPO, IFAD, UNIDO and the UN Tourism organisation; related organisations include the IAEA and WTO.

Significance: these bodies show the functionalist approach to international cooperation - solving practical problems in labour, health, food, development, communication and the environment builds habits of cooperation and benefits people directly. International administration thus extends beyond peace and security to human welfare, though agencies face challenges of funding, coordination and political influence.

Social Welfare Administration is the organisation and management of public and voluntary efforts designed to promote social well-being. Its scope includes welfare policies, institutions, programmes, personnel and services.

Social welfare in a narrow sense refers to services for vulnerable and disadvantaged groups - children, women, the elderly, persons with disabilities, the destitute and victims of social problems; in a broader sense, it includes all measures for the well-being of society, such as education, health, housing and social security. Social welfare administration is the process of organising and managing these services through policies, institutions, personnel and resources. Walter Friedlander defined social welfare as 'the organised system of social services and institutions designed to aid individuals and groups to attain satisfying standards of life and health'.

Scope: formulation of welfare policies; administration of welfare programmes and institutions (children's homes, women's shelters, old-age homes, rehabilitation centres); social legislation; financial administration of welfare funds; personnel administration (recruitment and training of social workers); coordination between government and voluntary agencies; research and evaluation; and public relations. In India, social welfare is mainly a State subject, but the Union plays a major role through the Ministries of Social Justice and Empowerment, Women and Child Development, Tribal Affairs and Minority Affairs, and centrally sponsored schemes. Article 38 and other Directive Principles provide the constitutional basis of the welfare state.
Social control refers to formal and informal means through which society regulates behaviour and maintains accepted norms.

Social control is the process by which society regulates the behaviour of individuals and groups to ensure conformity with norms, values and laws, and to maintain order and stability. The term was introduced by E. A. Ross ('Social Control', 1901). Types: (1) formal control - laws, police, courts, prisons, administrative regulations and organisational rules, enforced by authorised agencies with sanctions; and (2) informal control - customs, traditions, folkways, mores, religion, morality, public opinion, family, peer groups, ridicule, praise and gossip.

Agencies include the family, religion, education, community and state. Social control can be positive (rewards and encouragement) or negative (punishment). In traditional societies like Mizo villages, informal control through customary law, the chief, elders, Zawlbuk and later the church and the YMA has been very strong. Social welfare administration relates to social control through prevention of deviance, rehabilitation of offenders and addicts, and protection of vulnerable groups. Excessive social control may suppress individual freedom and minorities.
Social change means significant alteration in social relationships, institutions, values or patterns of life over time.

Social change is the alteration in social structure, institutions, relationships, values and patterns of behaviour over time (Kingsley Davis, MacIver and Page). Factors include technology and industrialisation, urbanisation, education, economic development, demographic changes, cultural contact and diffusion, ideology and social movements, legislation and state policies, religion, environment and globalisation. Theories include evolutionary (Spencer), cyclical (Spengler, Sorokin), conflict (Marx) and functionalist (Parsons) theories.

In India, processes of social change include Sanskritisation and Westernisation (M. N. Srinivas), modernisation, secularisation, urbanisation, the changing status of women, decline of the joint family, caste mobility and technological change (digital revolution). Social change creates new needs and problems - such as migration, family breakdown, care of the elderly, drug abuse, juvenile delinquency and domestic violence - which social welfare administration must address. Law and welfare policies can also be instruments of planned social change (for example, laws against untouchability, dowry and child marriage).
Juvenile delinquency refers to unlawful or seriously deviant behaviour by children or juveniles. Welfare administration emphasizes prevention, care, protection and rehabilitation.

Juvenile delinquency refers to offences or antisocial acts committed by children and adolescents below the age of 18 (in India, under the Juvenile Justice Act). Causes: family factors (broken homes, parental neglect, domestic violence, poverty, alcoholism of parents), peer pressure and gangs, school failure and dropout, urban slums and migration, unemployment, exposure to violence and media, drug abuse, lack of recreation, child labour and abuse, and mental health problems. Theories include Cohen's subculture theory, Sutherland's differential association theory, and Merton's strain theory.

Welfare approach: the juvenile justice system treats children in conflict with law differently from adults, focusing on reformation and rehabilitation rather than punishment. Measures include Juvenile Justice Boards, observation homes, special homes, probation, counselling, education and vocational training, foster care, after-care and community-based programmes. Prevention involves family support, schools, recreation, community programmes and child protection services (Mission Vatsalya). Data from the National Crime Records Bureau (NCRB) is used to monitor juvenile crime.
Drug addiction is harmful dependence on psychoactive substances and creates health, family and social problems requiring preventive, treatment and rehabilitation measures.

Drug addiction (substance use disorder) is a chronic condition in which a person compulsively uses substances such as alcohol, opioids (heroin, opium, prescription painkillers), cannabis, cocaine, methamphetamine and psychotropic drugs despite harmful consequences, with tolerance and withdrawal symptoms. The 2019 national survey 'Magnitude of Substance Use in India' (by AIIMS for the Ministry of Social Justice) found high rates of opioid use in Punjab, Haryana, Delhi, Mizoram, Manipur, Nagaland and other states. Mizoram, close to the 'Golden Triangle', has faced severe problems of heroin (locally called 'number four') and methamphetamine abuse, and high rates of HIV infection through injecting drug use.

Effects: physical and mental health problems, HIV and hepatitis, overdose deaths, crime, family breakdown, unemployment, poverty and stigma. Responses: the NDPS Act (1985); the National Action Plan for Drug Demand Reduction (2018-2025); the Nasha Mukt Bharat Abhiyaan (2020); de-addiction and rehabilitation centres (Integrated Rehabilitation Centres for Addicts, supported by the government and NGOs); harm reduction (opioid substitution therapy, needle exchange under the National AIDS Control Programme); awareness campaigns in schools and communities; and in Mizoram, the role of churches, the YMA and NGOs in rehabilitation and anti-drug campaigns.
Domestic violence includes abuse within domestic relationships and may take physical, emotional, sexual or economic forms.

Domestic violence is any act of abuse by a family member or intimate partner against another member, typically against women by husbands or in-laws, but also against children and the elderly. Forms: physical abuse (beating, burning), sexual abuse (including marital rape, which is not criminalised in India except in limited cases), verbal and emotional abuse (insults, threats, humiliation, controlling behaviour), and economic abuse (denying money, property or employment, forcing out of the home). Dowry-related harassment and dowry deaths are specific forms in India.

Causes: patriarchy and gender inequality, dowry, alcoholism, economic stress, social acceptance of violence, lack of awareness and legal support. According to the National Family Health Survey-5 (2019-2021), about 29 percent of ever-married women aged 18-49 reported experiencing spousal violence. Responses include laws (Section 498A of the IPC - now Section 85-86 of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023; the Dowry Prohibition Act, 1961; the Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005), One Stop Centres (Sakhi), women's helplines (181), protection officers, counselling centres, shelter homes (Swadhar Greh) and the work of NGOs and women's organisations such as the MHIP in Mizoram.
The Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015 provides a legal framework concerning children in conflict with law and children in need of care and protection.

The Juvenile Justice (Care and Protection of Children) Act, 2015, replaced the 2000 Act after debates following the 2012 Delhi gang rape, in which a juvenile was involved. It deals with two categories: (1) children in conflict with law (below 18, alleged or found to have committed an offence) and (2) children in need of care and protection (orphans, abandoned, abused, working or street children, children of addicts). A key provision allows children aged 16-18 accused of 'heinous offences' (punishable with seven years or more) to be tried as adults after a preliminary assessment of their mental and physical capacity by the Juvenile Justice Board; but no child can be sentenced to death or life imprisonment without the possibility of release.

Institutions: Juvenile Justice Boards (a Metropolitan or Judicial Magistrate and two social workers, one a woman) in each district for children in conflict with law; Child Welfare Committees (a chairperson and four members) for children in need of care and protection; Special Juvenile Police Units and Child Welfare Police Officers; observation homes, special homes, places of safety, children's homes, specialised adoption agencies and open shelters. It streamlined adoption procedures, with the Central Adoption Resource Authority (CARA) as a statutory body. Amendments in 2021 gave District Magistrates powers to issue adoption orders and supervise implementation. The Act is implemented under Mission Vatsalya (2021-2022, which subsumed the Integrated Child Protection Scheme).
The Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985 regulates and prohibits specified activities relating to narcotic drugs and psychotropic substances, subject to the law.

The Narcotic Drugs and Psychotropic Substances Act, 1985, consolidated laws on narcotic drugs (opium, cannabis, coca and their derivatives) and psychotropic substances (listed in schedules, such as LSD, amphetamines, barbiturates), in line with international conventions (the Single Convention on Narcotic Drugs 1961, the Convention on Psychotropic Substances 1971, and the UN Convention against Illicit Traffic 1988). It prohibits the cultivation, production, manufacture, possession, sale, purchase, transport, import, export and consumption of narcotic drugs and psychotropic substances, except for medical and scientific purposes under licence.

Features: punishments graded by quantity (small, intermediate and commercial quantities); severe penalties - rigorous imprisonment of 10-20 years for commercial quantities and the death penalty for repeat offences involving large quantities (Section 31A, made discretionary by a 2014 amendment); forfeiture of property derived from drug trafficking; restrictions on bail for serious offences (Section 37); Section 64A gives immunity from prosecution to addicts who volunteer for treatment; Section 71 allows the government to set up de-addiction centres; establishment of the Narcotics Control Bureau (1986) as the central coordinating agency; and amendments in 1989, 2001 and 2014 (the latter improved access to essential narcotic drugs for pain relief). Critics argue that the Act focuses too much on punishment of users and needs more emphasis on treatment and harm reduction.

sections.title: Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005

blocks.text: The Act provides legal protection and remedies for women facing domestic violence.

The Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 (PWDVA, in force from 26 October 2006) provides civil remedies to women facing domestic violence in a 'shared household' relationship - wives, live-in partners, sisters, mothers, daughters and widows. It defines domestic violence broadly to include physical, sexual, verbal, emotional and economic abuse, including harassment for dowry.

Institutions and procedure: Protection Officers appointed by state governments help women file a Domestic Incident Report and approach the Magistrate; Service Providers (registered NGOs) provide support; Magistrates can pass orders within 60 days: (1) protection orders (prohibiting further violence or contact); (2) residence orders (the right to reside in the shared household, regardless of ownership - strengthened by the Supreme Court in Satish Chander Ahuja, 2020); (3) monetary relief (expenses, maintenance, medical costs, loss of earnings); (4) custody orders for children; and (5) compensation orders. Violation of a protection order is a criminal offence punishable with imprisonment up to one year or a fine. In Hiral Harsora (2016), the Supreme Court allowed complaints against women members of the household too. Problems: inadequate protection officers, delays, lack of awareness and social stigma.
The CSWB was established to promote and support welfare activities, especially through voluntary organisations. The syllabus studies its organisation and functions.

The Central Social Welfare Board (CSWB) was set up by a resolution of the Government of India in August 1953, on the initiative of Dr Durgabai Deshmukh, who was its first chairperson. It was later registered as a charitable company under the Companies Act (1969) and functioned under the Ministry of Women and Child Development. Its aim was to promote social welfare activities and support voluntary organisations working for women, children and disadvantaged groups.

Organisation: a Chairperson, Board members (including representatives of ministries and experts in social welfare), and an executive director with staff. Functions: surveying welfare needs; promoting and developing voluntary social welfare organisations; providing grants-in-aid to voluntary agencies for programmes such as creches for children of working mothers, short-stay homes for women and girls, awareness generation programmes, condensed courses of education for adult women, family counselling centres, and welfare extension projects; coordinating welfare activities; and monitoring and evaluating programmes. Over time, many of its schemes were transferred to the ministry or other bodies, reducing its role; students should check the prescribed readings for its current status.
SSWABs functioned at the State level in coordination with welfare programmes and voluntary agencies. The syllabus examines their organisation and functions.

State Social Welfare Advisory Boards (SSWABs) were set up in states from 1954 to extend the CSWB's programmes at the state level. Each Board had a Chairperson (usually a non-official social worker appointed in consultation with the state government) and members including representatives of the state government, voluntary organisations, and the CSWB.

Functions: identifying the welfare needs of the state; recommending grants to voluntary organisations; inspecting and supervising the programmes of grantee institutions; implementing CSWB schemes (such as family counselling centres, awareness generation, creches and short-stay homes); coordinating welfare work between the state government, the CSWB and voluntary agencies; and advising on social welfare policy. Mizoram had a State Social Welfare Advisory Board working with voluntary organisations in the state.
The relationship involved coordination between central and state-level welfare bodies in implementing and supporting social welfare activities.

The relationship between the CSWB and SSWABs was based on partnership and coordination: the CSWB formulated schemes, provided funds and guidelines, and approved grants, while SSWABs identified needs, recommended voluntary organisations for assistance, implemented and supervised schemes, and reported to the CSWB. The administrative expenses of SSWABs were shared between the CSWB and state governments. The CSWB often worked through SSWABs as its field agencies.

Problems: dual control by the CSWB and state governments; delays in grants; inadequate staff and inspection; overlap with state social welfare departments; political appointments of chairpersons; and dependence of voluntary agencies on grants. Evaluations (such as by the Planning Commission) recommended clearer roles, stronger monitoring and better coordination. The relationship illustrates the importance of cooperation between central and state levels and between government and voluntary agencies in welfare administration.
Government formulates welfare policies, provides resources, creates institutions and implements or supports programmes for vulnerable groups.

Role of government: (1) policy-making - national policies for children (2013), women (2001), senior citizens (1999), persons with disabilities (2006) and others; (2) legislation - laws on child protection, women's rights, disability (Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act, 2016), senior citizens (Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act, 2007), transgender persons (2019), drug abuse and social security (Code on Social Security, 2020); (3) institutions - ministries and departments of social welfare at the Union and state levels, national commissions (NCW, NCPCR, NCSC, NCST), and statutory bodies; (4) financing - budget allocations, grants to states and voluntary organisations; (5) direct services - schemes such as ICDS, the National Social Assistance Programme (old-age, widow and disability pensions), scholarships, hostels, rehabilitation and skill programmes; and (6) monitoring and evaluation.

In Mizoram, the Social Welfare, Women and Child Development Department implements schemes for children, women, the elderly, persons with disabilities and drug rehabilitation. Government action is supplemented by voluntary agencies, community organisations and churches, which have long traditions of welfare work in Mizoram.
The Association for Voluntary Agencies for Rural Development represents the role of voluntary organisations in rural and social development.

AVARD (Association of Voluntary Agencies for Rural Development) was established in 1958 as a federation of voluntary organisations engaged in rural development, with leaders associated with the Gandhian and Sarvodaya movements; Jayaprakash Narayan was its early president. Its headquarters is in New Delhi.

Functions: promoting and coordinating voluntary action for rural development; providing information, training and research support to member agencies; organising seminars and conferences; acting as a link between voluntary organisations and the government (it was associated with planning for the role of voluntary agencies in Five-Year Plans); advocacy on issues such as rural poverty, panchayati raj, land reforms and people's participation; and publishing material on voluntary action. AVARD represents the role of voluntary organisations in complementing government efforts in social and rural development. Other national networks of voluntary organisations include CAPART (Council for Advancement of People's Action and Rural Technology, 1986, a government body that funded NGOs) and VANI (Voluntary Action Network India).

Social welfare personnel are trained workers and officials engaged in welfare programmes and services. Professional personnel are needed because welfare problems require specialised knowledge and skills.

Social welfare personnel include professional social workers (with degrees such as MSW from schools of social work - the first in India was the Sir Dorabji Tata Graduate School of Social Work, Bombay, 1936, now TISS), welfare officers, probation officers, child protection officers, counsellors, protection officers under the PWDVA, anganwadi workers and supervisors, caseworkers in institutions, and administrators in social welfare departments. Voluntary workers and community volunteers also contribute.

Professional skills required: knowledge of human behaviour and social problems, casework, group work and community organisation methods, counselling, research, administration, knowledge of social legislation, and ethics (confidentiality, respect for clients). Problems: shortage of trained personnel, low status and pay, lack of career prospects, appointment of untrained staff, heavy workloads and limited in-service training. Improving the quality of welfare personnel is essential for effective service delivery.

sections.title: Special Cadre for Social Welfare Personnel

blocks.text: A special cadre means a distinct professional service structure for social welfare personnel, intended to improve expertise, career development and effective welfare administration.

Several committees and experts have recommended a separate cadre (professional service) for social welfare personnel, with recruitment of trained social workers, defined career paths, promotions, in-service training and specialisation in areas such as child welfare, women's welfare, correctional services, disability and medical and psychiatric social work. The idea is that social welfare work requires professional knowledge, skills and attitudes, and should not be handled by general administrators who are frequently transferred.

Benefits: professionalism and expertise, continuity, better service quality, motivation through career prospects, and recognition of social work as a profession. Challenges: financial costs, small numbers of posts in some states, resistance from existing services, and the need for coordination with other departments. Some states have created social welfare or child protection services, and the JJ Act and other laws require trained officers, but a full special cadre has not been widely implemented.

sections.title: Meaning, Scope, Social Control, Change and Social Problems

blocks.text:
Social Welfare Administration organises welfare policies and services for the well-being of individuals and groups. It covers government agencies, voluntary organisations, personnel and programmes.

Social control maintains accepted behaviour through formal and informal mechanisms, while social change alters social institutions and relationships. Welfare administration must respond to changing social conditions.

The syllabus focuses on juvenile delinquency, drug addiction and domestic violence. These problems require not only legal action but also prevention, protection, rehabilitation and coordinated welfare services.

Meaning and scope: social welfare administration organises policies, programmes, institutions, personnel and resources to promote the well-being of individuals, groups and communities, especially vulnerable sections (children, women, elderly, persons with disabilities, SCs, STs, minorities and victims of social problems). It includes policy formulation, programme planning and implementation, institutional management, personnel and financial administration, coordination with voluntary agencies, research and evaluation. In India, it is grounded in the Directive Principles (Articles 38, 39, 41, 42, 46, 47) and implemented by central and state ministries.

Social control and social change: social control (formal through law and state agencies; informal through family, religion, community and public opinion) maintains social order; social change (through technology, urbanisation, education, economy, law and movements) transforms institutions and relationships, creating new welfare needs. Welfare administration must respond to changing conditions and sometimes acts as an agent of planned change.

Social problems: juvenile delinquency (causes - family breakdown, poverty, peer influence, drugs; responses - reformation and rehabilitation under the JJ Act), drug addiction (causes - availability, peer pressure, stress, unemployment; responses - NDPS Act, de-addiction, harm reduction, awareness; especially serious in Mizoram), and domestic violence (forms - physical, sexual, emotional and economic; responses - PWDVA, criminal law, One Stop Centres and helplines). These problems require integrated approaches combining law, prevention, protection, rehabilitation and community participation.

The Juvenile Justice Act, 2015 provides a framework for care, protection, rehabilitation and legal processes concerning children. The NDPS Act, 1985 regulates narcotic drugs and psychotropic substances and provides the legal framework for offences and control measures.

The Protection of Women from Domestic Violence Act, 2005 provides remedies and protection against domestic violence. Together, these laws show the close connection between welfare administration and social legislation.

Juvenile Justice Act, 2015: covers children in conflict with law and children in need of care and protection; Juvenile Justice Boards and Child Welfare Committees in every district; observation homes, special homes, children's homes and specialised adoption agencies; trial of 16-18-year-olds as adults for heinous offences after preliminary assessment; streamlined adoption through CARA; 2021 amendment empowering District Magistrates; rehabilitation and social reintegration through education, skills, foster care and after-care; implemented through Mission Vatsalya. NDPS Act, 1985: prohibits illicit drug activities except for medical and scientific purposes; graded punishments; forfeiture of property; Narcotics Control Bureau; treatment provisions (Section 64A immunity for addicts seeking treatment; de-addiction centres); criticised for criminalising users.

PWDVA, 2005: broad definition of domestic violence; protection officers and service providers; protection, residence, monetary relief, custody and compensation orders; quick relief from Magistrates within 60 days; violation punishable. Related laws include the Dowry Prohibition Act (1961), the Prohibition of Child Marriage Act (2006), the POCSO Act (2012), the Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace Act (2013), the Rights of Persons with Disabilities Act (2016) and the Maintenance and Welfare of Parents and Senior Citizens Act (2007).

Evaluation: social legislation provides the legal framework for welfare administration, protecting rights and creating institutions. However, implementation suffers from inadequate infrastructure and staff, lack of awareness, delays, social stigma and weak coordination. Effective welfare requires not only laws but trained personnel, resources, community participation and attitudinal change.

The Central Social Welfare Board and State Social Welfare Advisory Boards were important institutional arrangements for promoting welfare activities and cooperation with voluntary organisations. The central body operated at the national level while state boards linked welfare work with state-level needs.

Their relationship illustrates the need for coordination across levels of administration and between government and voluntary organisations in social welfare.

CSWB (1953): set up on Durgabai Deshmukh's initiative to promote voluntary social welfare; later a company under the Ministry of Women and Child Development; functions - surveying needs, promoting voluntary organisations, grants-in-aid for creches, short-stay homes, family counselling centres, condensed courses and awareness programmes, coordination, monitoring and evaluation. SSWABs (from 1954): state-level counterparts, recommending grants, implementing and supervising schemes, coordinating with state governments and voluntary agencies.

Relationship: the CSWB formulated schemes and provided funds; SSWABs identified needs, recommended grantees, supervised and reported; expenses were shared between the CSWB and states. Problems: dual control, delays in funds, overlap with state departments, inadequate monitoring and political appointments. Reforms recommended clearer roles, stronger monitoring and closer integration with government programmes.

Significance: the CSWB-SSWAB model was an innovative attempt to involve voluntary organisations and non-official social workers in welfare administration, combining government funding with voluntary initiative. It illustrates the need for coordination between levels of government and between government and civil society, though the welfare system has since shifted to larger centrally sponsored schemes and direct state implementation.

sections.title: Government, Voluntary Agencies and Welfare Personnel

blocks.text:
Government plays a central role through welfare policy, finance, institutions and programmes. Voluntary agencies supplement public action through community-level work and specialised services. AVARD is included in the syllabus as an example connected with voluntary rural development.

Social welfare personnel require professional skills because they work with complex social problems. The proposal for a special cadre seeks to strengthen professionalism, expertise and continuity in welfare administration.

Government: formulates policies, enacts legislation, establishes institutions (ministries, commissions, statutory bodies), finances programmes, provides direct services (ICDS, social security pensions, scholarships, rehabilitation, de-addiction) and monitors outcomes. The welfare state ideal of the Constitution makes government the main actor in social welfare, especially for large-scale needs.

Voluntary agencies: supplement government through community-level work, innovation, flexibility, specialised services, advocacy and mobilisation of local resources and volunteers; examples include AVARD (1958, a federation of voluntary agencies for rural development with Gandhian roots), national networks, and in Mizoram, churches, the YMA, MHIP and NGOs active in drug rehabilitation, HIV care and disaster relief. Problems include dependence on government grants, lack of accountability in some NGOs, and regulatory issues (the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act, amended 2020).

Personnel: social welfare requires trained professionals - social workers, counsellors, probation and protection officers - with skills in casework, group work, community organisation and counselling. Shortages, low status and lack of career prospects reduce effectiveness. A special cadre for social welfare personnel has been recommended to ensure professionalism, specialisation and continuity. Effective welfare administration therefore depends on partnership between government and voluntary agencies and on competent, motivated personnel.

sections.title: PUB 302 – PUBLIC FINANCIAL ADMINISTRATION IN INDIA
SHORT NOTES
context: PUB 302 – PUBLIC FINANCIAL ADMINISTRATION IN INDIA

sections.title: Financial Administration
context: PUB 302 – PUBLIC FINANCIAL ADMINISTRATION IN INDIA

blocks.text: Financial administration concerns the management of public revenue and expenditure. Its scope includes budgeting, accounting, audit, financial control and institutions responsible for public finance.

Financial administration is the 'life-blood' of administration because every activity requires money; Lloyd George said 'government is finance'. It includes the processes of raising revenue (taxes, fees, borrowing), allocating and spending money (budgeting), accounting, auditing, financial control and accountability. Definitions: L. D. White - 'the operations designed to make funds available to officials and to ensure their lawful and efficient use'.

Scope: (1) budgeting - preparation, enactment and execution of the budget; (2) accounting - recording transactions; (3) auditing - examining accounts for legality and propriety; (4) treasury management and cash management; (5) public debt management; (6) financial control by the executive, legislature and audit; (7) fiscal federalism - Union-state financial relations; and (8) institutions - the Ministry of Finance, RBI, Finance Commission, CAG and parliamentary committees. Constitutional provisions: Articles 112-117 (Union budget), 202-207 (state budgets), 264-293 (finance, property and contracts), 266-267 (Consolidated and Contingency Funds), 280 (Finance Commission), and 148-151 (CAG).

sections.title: Significance of Financial Administration
context: PUB 302 – PUBLIC FINANCIAL ADMINISTRATION IN INDIA

blocks.text: Sound financial administration helps ensure lawful use of public money, financial discipline, accountability and effective implementation of government programmes.

Significance: (1) it provides resources for all government activities and development programmes; (2) it ensures that public money is raised and spent lawfully and economically; (3) it is an instrument of economic policy - promoting growth, employment, price stability and redistribution through fiscal policy; (4) it enables legislative control over the executive ('no taxation without representation'); (5) it promotes accountability and transparency; (6) it helps planning and prioritisation of goals; (7) it supports federalism through the sharing of resources; and (8) it prevents waste, corruption and misuse of funds.

In India, financial administration is critical for a large welfare and development state, managing a Union budget of about 50 lakh crore rupees (2025-2026). Reforms such as the FRBM Act (2003), GST (2017), the Public Financial Management System, outcome budgeting and direct benefit transfers aim to improve fiscal discipline, efficiency and transparency.

sections.title: Budget
context: PUB 302 – PUBLIC FINANCIAL ADMINISTRATION IN INDIA

blocks.text: A budget is an annual financial statement of estimated government receipts and expenditure for a financial year.

The budget (from the French 'bougette', a leather bag) is called the 'Annual Financial Statement' in the Constitution (Article 112 for the Union, Article 202 for states). It is a statement of the estimated receipts and expenditure of the government for the financial year (1 April to 31 March). It distinguishes expenditure 'charged' on the Consolidated Fund (not voted - such as salaries of the President, judges, the CAG and debt charges) and 'voted' expenditure, and revenue and capital accounts.

Components: revenue budget (revenue receipts - tax and non-tax revenue; revenue expenditure - salaries, subsidies, interest, pensions) and capital budget (capital receipts - borrowings, disinvestment, loan recoveries; capital expenditure - assets, investment, loans). Deficits: revenue deficit, fiscal deficit (total expenditure minus total receipts excluding borrowings - the key indicator) and primary deficit (fiscal deficit minus interest payments). The budget is a financial, economic, political and administrative document - a plan of action, a means of control and an instrument of accountability.

sections.title: Principles of Budget
context: PUB 302 – PUBLIC FINANCIAL ADMINISTRATION IN INDIA

blocks.text: Budget principles seek clarity, comprehensiveness, proper authorisation, accountability and orderly financial management.

Principles (canons) of budgeting: (1) annuality - the budget covers one financial year, with unspent funds lapsing (the rule of lapse); (2) unity or comprehensiveness - all receipts and expenditure should be included in a single budget; (3) cash basis - estimates based on actual expected receipts and payments during the year; (4) gross budgeting - receipts and expenditure shown in full, not net; (5) accuracy and realism of estimates; (6) balanced budget or controlled deficit; (7) publicity and transparency; (8) legislative approval before expenditure - no money can be withdrawn from the Consolidated Fund without appropriation by law (Article 114); (9) specificity - funds should be spent only for the purposes approved; (10) flexibility within control (reappropriation under rules); and (11) accountability through accounts and audit.

Modern principles also include performance orientation (linking money to results), medium-term frameworks (the Medium-Term Fiscal Policy Statement under the FRBM Act), gender and environmental sensitivity, and participatory budgeting at local levels.

sections.title: Formulation of Budget
context: PUB 302 – PUBLIC FINANCIAL ADMINISTRATION IN INDIA

blocks.text: Budget formulation is the process through which departments prepare estimates and the government consolidates priorities and financial proposals before legislative consideration.

In India, the Budget Division of the Department of Economic Affairs in the Ministry of Finance prepares the Union budget. Steps: (1) the Budget Circular is issued around August-September with instructions and formats; (2) ministries and departments prepare estimates for the next year and revised estimates for the current year, based on estimates from field offices; (3) estimates are scrutinised by the Financial Advisers and the Department of Expenditure; (4) the Department of Revenue estimates tax receipts; (5) pre-budget consultations are held with stakeholders - industry, trade unions, economists, farmers and state finance ministers; (6) NITI Aayog and other bodies provide inputs; (7) the Finance Minister and Prime Minister decide on priorities and tax proposals; and (8) the Cabinet approves the budget just before presentation.

Presentation: the Finance Minister presents the budget in the Lok Sabha on 1 February (since 2017; earlier on the last working day of February); the Economic Survey is presented a day earlier; the separate Railway Budget was merged into the Union budget in 2017. Legislative stages: general discussion, scrutiny by Departmentally Related Standing Committees, voting on demands for grants (with cut motions), the guillotine, the Appropriation Bill and the Finance Bill. A vote on account is passed in election years.

sections.title: Line-Item Budget
context: PUB 302 – PUBLIC FINANCIAL ADMINISTRATION IN INDIA

blocks.text: A line-item budget classifies expenditure according to specific objects or items such as salaries, equipment and supplies. It emphasizes expenditure control.

The line-item (traditional or object-of-expenditure) budget classifies expenditure by items or objects - salaries, allowances, travel, office expenses, supplies, equipment and maintenance - for each department. It developed in the USA and Britain in the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries to control expenditure and prevent corruption.

Merits: simple to prepare and understand; ensures detailed financial control and accountability; prevents misuse by specifying the purpose of each item; and is easy to audit for legality. Demerits: focuses on inputs (what is bought) rather than outputs or outcomes (what is achieved); does not show the purpose or results of expenditure; encourages incrementalism (adding a percentage to last year's allocation); lacks long-term planning; and encourages year-end spending to avoid lapse ('March rush'). India's budget still largely follows this format at the department level, supplemented by outcome budgets.

sections.title: Performance Budget
context: PUB 302 – PUBLIC FINANCIAL ADMINISTRATION IN INDIA

blocks.text: Performance budgeting connects expenditure with functions, programmes, activities and results.

Performance budgeting, recommended by the first Hoover Commission in the USA (1949), presents the budget in terms of functions, programmes, activities and projects, showing the purposes of expenditure, costs and expected results (physical targets and performance indicators). It shifts the focus from 'what the government buys' to 'what the government does and achieves'.

In India, the first Administrative Reforms Commission (1966-1970) recommended performance budgeting; it was introduced in 1968-1969 for some ministries, and by 1977-1978 performance budgets were prepared by most development ministries. In 2005, the Outcome Budget was introduced, linking outlays to outputs and outcomes; since 2017-2018, the Output-Outcome Monitoring Framework (by NITI Aayog) has been used for major schemes. Merits: better planning, efficiency, accountability for results and transparency. Demerits: difficulty in measuring outputs and outcomes, especially in social sectors; complex; requires data and trained staff; and often becomes a formality.

sections.title: Zero-Based Budget
context: PUB 302 – PUBLIC FINANCIAL ADMINISTRATION IN INDIA

blocks.text: Zero-based budgeting requires programmes and expenditure to be justified afresh from a zero base rather than automatically continuing previous allocations.

Zero-based budgeting (ZBB) was developed by Peter Pyhrr at Texas Instruments (1969) and introduced in the US state of Georgia by Governor Jimmy Carter (1973) and later in the federal government (1977). It requires every programme and activity to be justified from scratch (zero base) each budget cycle, as if it were new, rather than assuming that existing allocations will continue. Steps: identifying 'decision units' (programmes or activities); preparing 'decision packages' with objectives, alternatives, costs and benefits at different funding levels; ranking packages in order of priority; and allocating resources according to the rankings.

In India, ZBB was introduced in the Department of Science and Technology (1983) and in all ministries from 1986-1987. Merits: eliminates obsolete and inefficient programmes, promotes efficient allocation, critical review, and accountability. Demerits: time-consuming and costly, requires large amounts of paperwork and data, difficult to apply to essential and committed expenditure (salaries, pensions, interest), and resistance from departments. In practice, it has been applied selectively or periodically rather than every year.

sections.title: Ministry of Finance
context: PUB 302 – PUBLIC FINANCIAL ADMINISTRATION IN INDIA

blocks.text: The Ministry of Finance is a central institution in Union financial administration and performs important functions relating to budgeting, revenue, expenditure and economic and financial policy.

The Ministry of Finance has five departments: Economic Affairs (Budget Division - preparation of the Union budget, the Economic Survey, external finance, currency and coinage, capital markets, infrastructure finance, and relations with the IMF, World Bank, ADB and G20); Expenditure (expenditure management, Financial Advisers in ministries, Pay Commission matters, the Controller General of Accounts, PFMS); Revenue (direct and indirect taxes through the Central Board of Direct Taxes and the Central Board of Indirect Taxes and Customs, the GST Council Secretariat, enforcement agencies such as the Enforcement Directorate); Financial Services (public sector banks, insurance, pensions - PFRDA, financial inclusion schemes such as Jan Dhan); and Investment and Public Asset Management (DIPAM - disinvestment).

Functions: formulating fiscal policy; preparing and implementing the budget; mobilising resources; controlling and monitoring expenditure (through Integrated Financial Advisers in each ministry); managing public debt (with the RBI); regulating financial institutions; administering taxation; coordinating Union-state financial relations; and representing India in international financial forums. It exercises 'financial control' over other ministries through prior approval of expenditure proposals and delegation of financial powers.

sections.title: Reserve Bank of India
context: PUB 302 – PUBLIC FINANCIAL ADMINISTRATION IN INDIA

blocks.text: The RBI is India's central bank. Its functions include monetary management, currency issue, banking regulation and acting as banker to government.

The Reserve Bank of India was established on 1 April 1935 under the RBI Act, 1934, on the recommendation of the Hilton Young Commission (1926), and nationalised on 1 January 1949. Headquarters: Mumbai. It is governed by a Central Board of Directors, headed by the Governor (Sanjay Malhotra since December 2024). Functions: (1) monetary authority - formulating and implementing monetary policy to maintain price stability while keeping growth in mind; since 2016, a six-member Monetary Policy Committee sets the policy repo rate to achieve the inflation target of 4 percent (plus or minus 2 percent); (2) issuer of currency (except one-rupee notes and coins, issued by the government); (3) regulator and supervisor of banks and non-banking financial companies; (4) manager of foreign exchange (Foreign Exchange Management Act, 1999) and foreign exchange reserves; (5) banker to the government - managing government accounts, public debt and ways and means advances; (6) banker's bank and lender of last resort; (7) regulator of payment and settlement systems (UPI is operated by NPCI under RBI oversight); and (8) developmental role - financial inclusion, priority sector lending, rural credit (through NABARD, 1982).

Instruments of monetary policy include the repo and reverse repo rates, the cash reserve ratio, statutory liquidity ratio, open market operations and the standing deposit facility. The RBI's autonomy and its relationship with the government (for example, debates over surplus transfers and the use of Section 7 of the RBI Act in 2018) are important issues in financial administration.

sections.title: Finance Commission
context: PUB 302 – PUBLIC FINANCIAL ADMINISTRATION IN INDIA

blocks.text: The Finance Commission is a constitutional body that recommends principles for distribution of specified financial resources between the Union and States and among States.

The Finance Commission (Article 280) is constituted by the President every five years (or earlier), consisting of a Chairman (with experience in public affairs) and four members (qualifications prescribed by the Finance Commission (Miscellaneous Provisions) Act, 1951). Functions: recommending (1) the distribution of the net proceeds of taxes between the Union and states (vertical devolution) and among states (horizontal distribution); (2) the principles governing grants-in-aid to states from the Consolidated Fund of India (Article 275); (3) measures to augment states' Consolidated Funds to supplement resources of panchayats and municipalities (added by the 73rd and 74th Amendments); and (4) any other matter referred by the President (such as disaster management funding and fiscal consolidation).

Recent commissions: the Fourteenth (Y. V. Reddy, 2015-2020) raised the states' share of the divisible pool from 32 to 42 percent; the Fifteenth (N. K. Singh, 2021-2026) recommended 41 percent (after the creation of the UTs of Jammu and Kashmir and Ladakh), using criteria such as population (2011), area, forest and ecology, income distance, demographic performance and tax effort; the Sixteenth (Arvind Panagariya, constituted in 2023) covers 2026-2031. Its recommendations are advisory but usually accepted. It is the 'balancing wheel of fiscal federalism'. Issues: the growing use of cesses and surcharges not shared with states, the role of the GST Council and NITI Aayog, and criteria disputes (such as southern states' concerns about population-based shares).

sections.title: Audit and Accounts
context: PUB 302 – PUBLIC FINANCIAL ADMINISTRATION IN INDIA

blocks.text: Accounts systematically record government financial transactions, while audit examines whether public money has been collected and spent according to law and prescribed rules.

Accounts: government accounts are kept in three parts - the Consolidated Fund (all revenues, loans raised and loan repayments; withdrawals need legislative appropriation), the Contingency Fund (for unforeseen expenditure pending legislative approval; at the disposal of the President or Governor) and the Public Account (money held in trust, such as provident funds, small savings and deposits). In 1976, accounts were separated from audit at the Union level (departmentalisation of accounts), with the Controller General of Accounts (CGA) in the Department of Expenditure preparing accounts, supported by Pay and Accounts Offices; the PFMS (Public Financial Management System) tracks fund flows. In most states, accounts are still compiled by the Accountants General under the CAG.
