Audit: independent examination of accounts and financial transactions to ensure they comply with laws, rules and sanctions, and that public money is used economically, efficiently and effectively. Types: compliance or regularity audit (legality), propriety audit (wisdom, faithfulness and economy), financial audit (accuracy of accounts and financial statements), performance audit (economy, efficiency and effectiveness of programmes) and, increasingly, IT audit, environmental audit and social audit (by communities, for MGNREGA). Internal audit is conducted by departments; external audit by the CAG. Audit helps legislative control and accountability.

sections.title: CAG
context: PUB 302 – PUBLIC FINANCIAL ADMINISTRATION IN INDIA

blocks.text: The Comptroller and Auditor General of India is the constitutional authority responsible for auditing specified public accounts and reporting audit findings according to the Constitution and law.

The Comptroller and Auditor General (Articles 148-151) is appointed by the President by warrant for six years or until age 65, whichever is earlier. Independence is protected: removal only in the manner of a Supreme Court judge (special majority of both Houses on grounds of proved misbehaviour or incapacity); salary and service conditions determined by Parliament and not varied to the CAG's disadvantage; expenses charged on the Consolidated Fund; and ineligibility for further government office after tenure. The CAG heads the Indian Audit and Accounts Department. The CAG's (Duties, Powers and Conditions of Service) Act, 1971, defines duties.

Functions: auditing all expenditure from the Consolidated Funds of India and the states (and Union Territories with legislatures), Contingency Funds and Public Accounts; auditing trading, manufacturing and profit-and-loss accounts of government departments; auditing government companies and corporations (with statutory corporations audited as per their laws); auditing bodies substantially financed by government grants; advising the President on the form of accounts (Article 150); and submitting audit reports to the President and Governors, which are laid before Parliament and state legislatures (Article 151) and examined by the Public Accounts Committee. Ambedkar called the CAG 'probably the most important officer in the Constitution of India'. Notable reports: 2G spectrum (2010), Commonwealth Games (2011), coal blocks (2012). Limitations: post-facto audit, no power to stop expenditure or punish, limited audit of secret service funds and private entities in PPPs.

sections.title: Public Accounts Committee
context: PUB 302 – PUBLIC FINANCIAL ADMINISTRATION IN INDIA

blocks.text: The PAC examines public accounts and CAG reports and helps the legislature scrutinise government expenditure.

The Public Accounts Committee (PAC) was first set up in 1921 under the Montagu-Chelmsford Reforms. It has 22 members - 15 from the Lok Sabha and 7 from the Rajya Sabha - elected annually by proportional representation by single transferable vote. Ministers cannot be members. Since 1967, by convention, its chairman is from the opposition, appointed by the Speaker. States have their own PACs.

Functions: examining the appropriation accounts and finance accounts of the Union government and the CAG's audit reports; ascertaining whether money granted by Parliament was spent within its scope and for the purposes intended; examining the accounts of autonomous bodies and corporations (other than those under the Committee on Public Undertakings); and investigating cases of excess expenditure, waste, extravagance, losses and irregularities. It examines officials as witnesses and submits reports with recommendations to Parliament; the government submits action-taken notes. The CAG acts as its 'friend, philosopher and guide'. Limitations: post-mortem examination of past expenditure, no power to enforce recommendations, and it cannot intervene in policy questions. It is considered the most important financial committee, ensuring accountability.

sections.title: Estimates Committee
context: PUB 302 – PUBLIC FINANCIAL ADMINISTRATION IN INDIA

blocks.text: The Estimates Committee examines budget estimates and suggests economy, efficiency and improvements in administration.

The Estimates Committee originated from the Standing Financial Committee (1921); the first Estimates Committee after independence was set up in 1950 on the recommendation of John Mathai, the Finance Minister. It has 30 members, all from the Lok Sabha, elected annually by proportional representation; ministers are excluded. The chairman is appointed by the Speaker from among the members, usually from the ruling party. It is the largest parliamentary committee.

Functions: examining the budget estimates of ministries and departments selected by it each year, and reporting on: what economies, improvements in organisation, efficiency or administrative reform can be effected consistent with the policy underlying the estimates; suggesting alternative policies to bring about efficiency and economy in administration; examining whether money is well laid out within the limits of the policy; and suggesting the form in which the estimates should be presented to Parliament. It is called a 'continuous economy committee'. Limitations: it examines estimates after they are voted (its work runs throughout the year, not before voting); it cannot question policy laid down by Parliament; its recommendations are advisory; and it selects only some ministries each year. Since 1993, Departmentally Related Standing Committees examine demands for grants before voting, which has reduced its importance.

sections.title: Committee on Public Undertakings
context: PUB 302 – PUBLIC FINANCIAL ADMINISTRATION IN INDIA

blocks.text: The Committee on Public Undertakings examines matters relating to public sector undertakings within its parliamentary mandate.

The Committee on Public Undertakings (COPU) was created in 1964 on the recommendation of the Krishna Menon Committee. It has 22 members - 15 from the Lok Sabha and 7 from the Rajya Sabha - elected annually; ministers are excluded; the chairman is appointed by the Speaker from the Lok Sabha members.

Functions: examining the reports and accounts of public sector undertakings (PSUs) specified in the Fourth Schedule of the Rules of Procedure (such as ONGC, NTPC, SAIL, BHEL, Coal India); examining CAG reports on PSUs; examining whether the affairs of PSUs are managed according to sound business principles and prudent commercial practices; and examining their autonomy and efficiency. Limitations: it does not examine major government policy questions, day-to-day administration or matters for which other machinery exists (such as matters of collective bargaining); it can examine only a limited number of PSUs each year; and its recommendations are advisory. With privatisation and disinvestment, the scope of PSUs has changed, but COPU remains important for parliamentary oversight of public enterprises.

sections.title: LONG NOTES
context: PUB 302 – PUBLIC FINANCIAL ADMINISTRATION IN INDIA

sections.title: Financial Administration and Budget Formulation
context: PUB 302 – PUBLIC FINANCIAL ADMINISTRATION IN INDIA

blocks.text:
Public Financial Administration deals with government revenue, expenditure, budgeting, accounting and audit. Its significance lies in ensuring that public money is raised and spent lawfully, economically and in accordance with public policy.

The budget is the government's annual financial statement of expected receipts and expenditure. Good budgeting requires clarity, comprehensiveness, proper authorisation and accountability. Budget formulation begins with departmental estimates and develops into a consolidated governmental financial plan for legislative consideration.

Financial administration: management of public revenue and expenditure through budgeting, accounting, auditing, treasury and debt management, and financial control; constitutional framework (Articles 112-117, 202-207, 264-293, 148-151, 280); significance - provides resources, ensures legality and economy, instrument of fiscal policy, legislative control, accountability, planning and fiscal federalism. Budget: the Annual Financial Statement; revenue and capital budgets; charged and voted expenditure; deficits (revenue, fiscal, primary).

Principles of budgeting: annuality and rule of lapse, unity, cash basis, gross budgeting, accuracy, balance, publicity, legislative approval, specificity and accountability; modern principles of performance orientation, medium-term frameworks and gender sensitivity. Formulation: budget circular; estimates by departments; scrutiny by financial advisers and the Department of Expenditure; revenue estimates; pre-budget consultations; decisions by the Finance Minister and Prime Minister; Cabinet approval; presentation on 1 February with the Economic Survey.

Enactment and execution: general discussion; scrutiny by DRSCs; voting on demands for grants and cut motions; guillotine; Appropriation and Finance Bills; vote on account; release of funds and expenditure control; supplementary and excess grants; accounting and audit; and examination by the PAC. The FRBM Act (2003) sets fiscal targets. Reforms include outcome budgeting, gender budgeting, GST, PFMS and DBT. Sound financial administration ensures that public money serves public purposes lawfully, efficiently and accountably.

sections.title: Types of Budget
context: PUB 302 – PUBLIC FINANCIAL ADMINISTRATION IN INDIA

blocks.text:
A line-item budget classifies expenditure by objects such as salaries and supplies and is useful for financial control. Performance budgeting connects money with programmes, activities and results and therefore places greater emphasis on what expenditure achieves.

Zero-based budgeting requires expenditure proposals to be justified afresh instead of assuming that previous spending should automatically continue. Each method therefore emphasizes a different aspect of financial management.

Line-item budget: classifies expenditure by objects (salaries, travel, supplies); emphasises control, accountability and legality; simple and easy to audit; but focuses on inputs, ignores results, encourages incrementalism and year-end spending. Performance budget: classifies expenditure by functions, programmes and activities with physical targets and performance measures (Hoover Commission, 1949; India from 1968-1969; Outcome Budget 2005; Output-Outcome Monitoring Framework 2017); emphasises management, efficiency and results; but outputs and outcomes are hard to measure and it may become a formality.

Zero-based budget: every programme justified from zero each cycle (Peter Pyhrr, 1969; Jimmy Carter in Georgia; India from 1986-1987); decision units, decision packages and ranking; emphasises priority-setting and elimination of obsolete programmes; but time-consuming, data-intensive and difficult for committed expenditure. Other types: Planning-Programming-Budgeting System (PPBS, US Department of Defense under Robert McNamara, 1961), linking planning and budgeting through cost-benefit analysis; outcome budgeting; gender budgeting; green budgeting; and participatory budgeting (Porto Alegre, Brazil, 1989).

Comparison: the evolution from line-item to performance and zero-based budgeting reflects a shift in emphasis from control (are funds spent legally?) to management (are funds spent efficiently?) to planning and priority-setting (are funds spent on the right things?). Modern budgeting combines these, using line-item control for accountability with outcome measures for performance and periodic zero-based reviews for priorities.

sections.title: Financial Institutions
context: PUB 302 – PUBLIC FINANCIAL ADMINISTRATION IN INDIA

blocks.text:
The Ministry of Finance plays a central role in Union budgeting, expenditure, revenue and financial policy. The Reserve Bank of India performs central banking functions, including monetary management, currency issue, banking regulation and services to government.

The Finance Commission is a constitutional body concerned with federal financial relations. It recommends principles for sharing specified resources between the Union and States and among States.

Ministry of Finance: five departments (Economic Affairs, Expenditure, Revenue, Financial Services, DIPAM); prepares and implements the budget, formulates fiscal policy, mobilises resources, controls expenditure through Integrated Financial Advisers and delegated financial powers, manages public debt, administers taxation (CBDT, CBIC, GST Council), regulates financial institutions and represents India internationally. It is the central coordinating institution of financial administration.

Reserve Bank of India: central bank (1935, nationalised 1949); monetary policy through the Monetary Policy Committee (inflation targeting since 2016); currency issue; regulation and supervision of banks and NBFCs; foreign exchange management; banker to the government (managing accounts, debt, ways and means advances); banker's bank and lender of last resort; payment systems; and developmental functions (financial inclusion, priority sector lending). Its autonomy from the government is important for credibility.

Finance Commission: constitutional body (Article 280) constituted every five years; recommends vertical and horizontal distribution of central taxes, grants-in-aid to states, measures for local bodies' finances and other matters; the Fifteenth Commission recommended 41 percent devolution to states; the Sixteenth covers 2026-2031. Together, these institutions manage India's fiscal system - the Ministry of Finance handles fiscal policy, the RBI monetary policy and the Finance Commission fiscal federalism. The GST Council (2016) has become another key institution of cooperative fiscal federalism.

sections.title: Audit, CAG and Parliamentary Control
context: PUB 302 – PUBLIC FINANCIAL ADMINISTRATION IN INDIA

blocks.text:
Public accounts record financial transactions, while audit checks their legality, regularity and financial propriety. The Comptroller and Auditor General is the constitutional audit authority for specified public accounts.

Parliamentary committees strengthen legislative control. The Public Accounts Committee examines accounts and audit reports, the Estimates Committee examines estimates and possibilities for economy and efficiency, and the Committee on Public Undertakings scrutinises public enterprises within its mandate.

Accounts and audit: government accounts are maintained in the Consolidated Fund, Contingency Fund and Public Account; at the Union level, accounts were departmentalised (1976) under the Controller General of Accounts, while audit is the CAG's responsibility. Audit types - compliance, propriety, financial, performance, IT, environmental and social audit. The CAG (Articles 148-151): appointed for six years or until 65; removable like a Supreme Court judge; audits Union and state accounts, PSUs and grant-receiving bodies; reports to the President and Governors; acts as the 'friend, philosopher and guide' of the PAC; limitations - post-facto audit, no enforcement powers.

Parliamentary financial committees: the Public Accounts Committee (22 members, opposition chairman by convention) examines appropriation and finance accounts and CAG reports, investigating irregularities and waste; the Estimates Committee (30 Lok Sabha members) examines estimates and suggests economies and efficiency ('continuous economy committee'); the Committee on Public Undertakings (22 members) examines the reports, accounts and CAG reports on PSUs. Departmentally Related Standing Committees (since 1993) examine demands for grants before voting.

Evaluation: this system of executive control, independent audit and legislative scrutiny establishes financial accountability. Limitations include post-facto scrutiny, delays in considering reports, non-implementation of recommendations, limited time for budget discussion (much expenditure is passed by guillotine), and the growing complexity of finances (PPPs, off-budget borrowing). Reforms suggested include timely action on audit reports, strengthening committees, more time for budget scrutiny and better transparency of off-budget liabilities.

Civil society refers to voluntary associations and organised social activity existing between the individual, market and State. It includes organisations through which citizens pursue shared interests and public causes.

Civil society is the sphere of voluntary associations, organisations and networks outside the family, the market and the state, through which citizens pursue common interests and public causes. It includes NGOs, community-based organisations, trade unions, professional associations, cooperatives, religious organisations, student and youth groups, women's organisations, social movements, think tanks, media and informal networks. Features: voluntary membership, autonomy from the state, non-profit orientation (mostly), pluralism, and participation in public life.

Functions: representing and advocating citizens' interests; providing services (health, education, relief); monitoring government and demanding accountability; mobilising people and building social movements; promoting democratic values, tolerance and participation; and creating social capital. In Mizoram, civil society is strong - the YMA, MHIP, MZP, MUP, churches and NGOs play major roles in community service and public affairs.
The idea developed through political thought concerning society, citizenship and the relationship between State and non-State associations.

The concept has a long history. Classical thinkers (Aristotle's 'koinonia politike', Cicero's 'societas civilis') used it to mean political community. Social contract thinkers (Hobbes, Locke, Rousseau) contrasted civil (political) society with the state of nature. Adam Ferguson ('An Essay on the History of Civil Society', 1767) and the Scottish Enlightenment linked it with commerce and refinement. Hegel ('Philosophy of Right', 1821) distinguished civil society (the sphere of economic needs, market, self-interest and associations) from the family and the state.

Marx saw civil society as the sphere of bourgeois economic relations. Alexis de Tocqueville ('Democracy in America', 1835-1840) emphasised voluntary associations as schools of democracy that check government power. Antonio Gramsci saw civil society as the sphere of culture and ideology where the ruling class establishes hegemony, but also where counter-hegemonic struggles occur. In the late twentieth century, the concept was revived by movements against communism in Eastern Europe (Solidarity in Poland), by Jürgen Habermas (the public sphere) and by development agencies (World Bank), which promoted NGOs and participation. In India, civil society includes traditions of social reform, the freedom movement, Gandhian constructive work and modern NGOs and movements.
Social capital refers to networks, trust and norms of cooperation that help people act collectively.

Social capital refers to the networks, norms of reciprocity and trust that enable people to cooperate for mutual benefit. Key theorists: Pierre Bourdieu (social capital as resources linked to networks and group membership that individuals use for advantage); James Coleman (social capital as a public good facilitating action, especially in education); and Robert Putnam ('Making Democracy Work', 1993, comparing northern and southern Italy; and 'Bowling Alone', 2000, on the decline of civic participation in the USA), who argued that regions with strong civic traditions and associations had better-performing governments and economies.

Types (Putnam and Michael Woolcock): bonding social capital (ties within homogeneous groups - family, clan, ethnic or religious community), bridging social capital (ties across different groups) and linking social capital (ties with people in power and institutions). Benefits: cooperation, collective action, information flow, reduced transaction costs, better governance and well-being. Negative aspects: exclusion of outsiders, nepotism, pressure to conform and sectarianism. In Mizoram, strong bonding social capital through tlawmngaihna, the YMA and churches supports community action, though inclusion of minorities requires bridging social capital.
Civil society organisations can create social capital by building trust, participation and networks of cooperation.

Civil society organisations create social capital by bringing people together, building trust, developing norms of cooperation and reciprocity, and training citizens in participation, leadership and democratic skills - Tocqueville's idea of associations as 'schools of democracy'. Examples: self-help groups building trust and mutual credit among women; cooperatives; neighbourhood associations; religious and youth groups organising community service; and social movements creating networks of solidarity.

In turn, social capital strengthens civil society by making collective action easier. Together they contribute to good governance by improving accountability, service delivery (community participation in schools, health and water management), conflict resolution and resilience in disasters. Putnam's research suggested that civic engagement improves government performance. However, not all associations build bridging social capital; some reinforce divisions. Policies that support inclusive associations, participatory governance and trust-building strengthen both civil society and social capital.
Civil society has played an important role in demanding transparency and using the Right to Information framework to promote accountability in India.

The Right to Information movement in India began in the early 1990s with the Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan (MKSS), founded in 1990 by Aruna Roy, Nikhil Dey and Shankar Singh in Rajasthan. Its jan sunwais (public hearings) from 1994 exposed corruption in local development works and wage payments by reading out official records in villages, with the slogan 'Hamara paisa, hamara hisab' (Our money, our accounts). The National Campaign for People's Right to Information (NCPRI, 1996), journalists, lawyers and activists joined. The Supreme Court had held that the right to information is part of freedom of speech (Article 19(1)(a)) and the right to life (State of UP v. Raj Narain, 1975; S. P. Gupta, 1981).

States such as Tamil Nadu (1997), Goa (1997), Rajasthan (2000), Maharashtra and Delhi passed RTI laws; the central Freedom of Information Act (2002) was weak; and the Right to Information Act, 2005 (in force from 12 October 2005) was passed by the UPA government, with input from the National Advisory Council. Features: any citizen can request information from public authorities, which must reply within 30 days (48 hours if life or liberty is involved); Public Information Officers; proactive disclosure (Section 4); exemptions (Section 8, such as national security and privacy); Information Commissions at the Centre and states. Civil society uses RTI to expose corruption, monitor schemes and empower citizens. Challenges: attacks on RTI activists, pendency in Information Commissions, the 2019 amendment allowing the central government to set the tenure and salaries of Information Commissioners, and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act (2023) amendment to Section 8(1)(j).
Self Help Groups organise members around savings, credit and collective activity and can strengthen women's participation and economic capacity.

Self-help groups (SHGs) are small voluntary groups of 10-20 people, usually women from similar socio-economic backgrounds, who save regularly, lend to members from their pooled savings, and access bank credit as a group without collateral. The SHG-Bank Linkage Programme was launched by NABARD in 1992, inspired by experiments such as MYRADA in Karnataka and the Grameen Bank of Muhammad Yunus in Bangladesh. SHGs are supported under the National Rural Livelihoods Mission (NRLM, 2011, renamed DAY-NRLM - 'Aajeevika') and DAY-NULM in urban areas. India has over 90 lakh SHGs with about 10 crore women members. Kerala's Kudumbashree (1998) is a celebrated model.

Benefits for women: financial inclusion and savings; access to credit for livelihoods (agriculture, livestock, handicrafts, small businesses); increased income and economic independence; confidence, leadership and decision-making in families and communities; collective action on social issues (alcoholism, domestic violence, health and sanitation); and participation in local governance (many SHG members have become panchayat representatives). Challenges: small loan sizes, dependence on subsidies, elite capture, debt burdens, limited markets and skills, and the double burden of work. In Mizoram, SHGs under the Mizoram State Rural Livelihoods Mission support women's livelihoods.
Gender budgeting examines public budgets from the perspective of their impact on women and gender equality.

Gender budgeting is the application of gender analysis to budgets - examining how government expenditure and revenue affect women and men differently, and allocating resources to promote gender equality. It does not mean a separate budget for women. It began in Australia (1984) and gained momentum after the Beijing Platform for Action (1995). In India, a Gender Budget Statement has been included in the Union budget since 2005-2006, with Part A (schemes with 100 percent allocation for women) and Part B (schemes with at least 30 percent allocation for women); Gender Budgeting Cells were set up in ministries. In 2024-2025, the allocation shown in the Gender Budget Statement was over 3 lakh crore rupees, about 6.5 percent of total expenditure.

Tools include gender-disaggregated beneficiary analysis, gender audits of policies, gender-sensitive indicators and outcome assessment. Many states also prepare gender budgets. Merits: makes the needs of women visible, improves targeting and accountability, and mainstreams gender in policy. Criticisms: often a formality, based on rough estimates; lack of gender-disaggregated data; focus on allocation rather than outcomes; and limited impact on mainstream sectors such as infrastructure.
Reservation is used as a measure to improve women's representation in political and public institutions.

Women's political representation in India has been low: women made up about 13.6 percent of Lok Sabha members after the 2024 elections (74 MPs) and about 9-10 percent in state assemblies on average. To address this, the 73rd and 74th Amendments (1992) reserved not less than one-third of seats and chairperson posts in panchayats and municipalities for women; about 21 states have increased this to 50 percent. As a result, over 14 lakh women serve as elected representatives in local bodies.

The Constitution (106th Amendment) Act, 2023 (the Nari Shakti Vandan Adhiniyam) reserves one-third of seats in the Lok Sabha, state legislative assemblies and the Delhi assembly for women, including within seats reserved for SCs and STs, for 15 years. It will come into effect after the next census and delimitation. Debates: whether OBC women should have a sub-quota; whether reservation leads to 'proxy' representation (sarpanch-pati); the delay in implementation; and whether parties should give more tickets to women voluntarily. Studies (such as Chattopadhyay and Duflo, 2004) found that women leaders in panchayats invested more in drinking water and roads, issues important to women. Reservation in education and jobs for women also exists in some states (such as 33 percent in police in several states).

sections.title: National Policy for Empowerment of Women, 2001

blocks.text: The policy sought advancement, development and empowerment of women through a broad national policy framework.

The National Policy for the Empowerment of Women (2001), adopted by the Department of Women and Child Development (2001 was declared the 'Year of Women's Empowerment'), aimed at the advancement, development and empowerment of women. Objectives: creating an environment through positive economic and social policies for the full development of women; de jure and de facto enjoyment of human rights and fundamental freedoms; equal access to participation and decision-making in social, political and economic life; equal access to health care, education, employment, social security and public office; strengthening legal systems to eliminate discrimination; changing social attitudes through active participation of men and women; mainstreaming a gender perspective in development; elimination of violence and discrimination against women and girls; and partnerships with civil society, especially women's organisations.

Strategies: gender-sensitive policies, laws and programmes; economic empowerment (poverty eradication, microcredit, women in agriculture and industry); social empowerment (education, health, nutrition, drinking water, housing, environment); attention to women in difficult circumstances; and institutional mechanisms (national and state commissions, gender budgeting). A draft National Policy for Women was prepared in 2016 but not formally adopted. Institutions such as the Ministry of Women and Child Development (2006) and the National Commission for Women (1992) implement related programmes.
Integrated Child Development Services provides a package of services relating to nutrition, health and early childhood development.

The Integrated Child Development Services (ICDS) scheme was launched on 2 October 1975 in 33 blocks and has become one of the world's largest programmes for early childhood development. It targets children aged 0-6 years, pregnant women and lactating mothers, and adolescent girls (under certain components). Six services: supplementary nutrition (take-home rations and hot cooked meals), pre-school non-formal education (for children aged 3-6), nutrition and health education, immunisation, health check-ups and referral services (the last three through the health system).

Delivery is through Anganwadi Centres (about 14 lakh), run by Anganwadi Workers and Helpers, supervised by Supervisors and Child Development Project Officers. The National Food Security Act (2013) made supplementary nutrition a legal entitlement. In 2021-2022, ICDS components were restructured under 'Mission Saksham Anganwadi and Poshan 2.0', integrating the POSHAN Abhiyaan (2018), the Scheme for Adolescent Girls and anganwadi services, with digital monitoring through the Poshan Tracker. Achievements include reduced malnutrition and improved immunisation, but challenges remain: high rates of stunting (35.5 percent in NFHS-5), poor infrastructure, low honoraria for workers, and quality of food and pre-school education.
Integrated Child Protection Services is included in the syllabus as an institutional programme concerned with child protection.

The Integrated Child Protection Scheme (ICPS), launched in 2009-2010 by the Ministry of Women and Child Development, aimed to build a protective environment for children in difficult circumstances, by consolidating earlier schemes (programmes for juvenile justice, street children and adoption) and supporting the implementation of the Juvenile Justice Act. In 2021-2022, ICPS was subsumed under 'Mission Vatsalya' (the Child Protection Services Scheme), with similar objectives.

Components: establishing statutory bodies (Juvenile Justice Boards, Child Welfare Committees, Special Juvenile Police Units); service delivery structures (State Child Protection Societies, District Child Protection Units headed by District Child Protection Officers); institutional care (children's homes, observation homes, special homes, specialised adoption agencies, open shelters); non-institutional care (sponsorship, foster care, adoption, after-care); the CHILDLINE helpline (1098, now integrated with the Emergency Response Support System 112); training and capacity-building; and data management (the Track Child portal for missing children). It focuses on prevention, protection and rehabilitation of children in need of care and protection and children in conflict with law.
The policy provides a national framework recognising children's rights, survival, health, development, protection and participation.

The National Policy for Children (2013), adopted on 26 April 2013 by the Ministry of Women and Child Development, replaced the 1974 policy. It defines a child as anyone below 18, recognises every child as a unique and supreme national asset, and affirms the rights-based approach of the UN Convention on the Rights of the Child. Guiding principles: universal and inalienable rights; equal treatment and non-discrimination; best interests of the child; family as the best environment; safety and protection from harm; children's participation; and inter-sectoral convergence.

Four key priority areas: (1) survival, health and nutrition (reducing infant and maternal mortality, malnutrition, immunisation); (2) education and development (early childhood care, free and compulsory education under the RTE Act, quality education, skills); (3) protection (from abuse, exploitation, child labour, trafficking, child marriage, violence and neglect, including children in difficult circumstances such as disasters and conflict); and (4) participation (children's right to express views and be heard). It requires a National Plan of Action (2016) and coordination among ministries, states, local bodies and civil society, monitored by the National Coordination and Action Group. The National Commission for Protection of Child Rights (2007) and state commissions monitor child rights.
Human rights are basic rights and freedoms belonging to human beings by virtue of being human.

Human rights are inherent, universal, inalienable, indivisible and interdependent rights of all people based on human dignity, including civil and political rights (life, liberty, equality, fair trial, expression, religion, association, participation) and economic, social and cultural rights (work, education, health, food, housing, social security, culture), as well as collective rights (self-determination, development, environment).

In India, human rights are protected through the Constitution (Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles), laws, the judiciary (writs, PIL, expansive interpretation of Article 21), national and state human rights commissions, other national commissions (women, children, SCs, STs, minorities), and civil society. Human rights administration involves protecting citizens from abuses by the state (custodial violence, illegal detention) and non-state actors, and promoting conditions for a dignified life.
The Universal Declaration of Human Rights, adopted in 1948, sets out a broad international statement of fundamental human rights and freedoms.

The Universal Declaration of Human Rights was adopted by the UN General Assembly in Paris on 10 December 1948 (Human Rights Day), drafted by the Commission on Human Rights chaired by Eleanor Roosevelt, with René Cassin, Charles Malik, P. C. Chang, John Humphrey and India's Hansa Mehta (who ensured the language 'All human beings are born free and equal in dignity and rights'). It has a Preamble and 30 articles covering civil, political, economic, social and cultural rights.

It is not a legally binding treaty, but it has become the foundation of international human rights law, much of it accepted as customary international law, and inspired the ICCPR and ICESCR (1966), regional human rights systems and national constitutions, including India's. It is the most translated document in the world. It is used by courts, governments, NGOs and human rights institutions as a standard.
The National Human Rights Commission is an institution for protection and promotion of human rights in India under the relevant legal framework.

The NHRC was established on 12 October 1993 under the Protection of Human Rights Act, 1993 (amended 2006 and 2019), following the Paris Principles. Composition (2019 amendment): a Chairperson who has been Chief Justice of India or a Supreme Court judge; a member who is or has been a Supreme Court judge; a member who is or has been a Chief Justice of a High Court; three members with knowledge of human rights (at least one woman); and ex officio members (chairpersons of the national commissions for SCs, STs, women, minorities, backward classes, child rights, and the Chief Commissioner for Persons with Disabilities). Appointment by the President on the recommendation of a committee headed by the Prime Minister; term of three years or until 70.

Functions: inquiry into complaints of human rights violations by public servants (suo motu or on petition); intervention in court proceedings; visits to prisons and institutions; review of laws and safeguards; study of treaties; research; human rights literacy; and support to NGOs. Powers of a civil court for investigation; recommendations for compensation and prosecution. Limitations: recommendations are not binding; one-year limit on complaints; limited powers over armed forces; dependence on government. It has addressed custodial deaths (guidelines requiring reporting within 24 hours), encounter killings, bonded labour, manual scavenging and the rights of persons with mental illness.
State Human Rights Commissions perform human-rights protection functions at the State level where constituted.

Under the Protection of Human Rights Act, state governments may constitute State Human Rights Commissions (SHRCs). Composition (after 2019): a Chairperson who has been Chief Justice or a judge of a High Court, and two members (a serving or retired High Court judge or district judge with seven years' experience, and a person with knowledge of human rights). Members are appointed by the Governor on the recommendation of a committee headed by the Chief Minister (including the Speaker, the state Home Minister and the Leader of Opposition), but can be removed only by the President. Term: three years or until age 70.

Functions: inquiring into violations of human rights in matters relating to subjects in the State and Concurrent Lists; visiting jails and institutions; reviewing safeguards; promoting human rights awareness; and recommending compensation and action. If the NHRC is already inquiring into a matter, the SHRC cannot take it up. Most states have SHRCs, including Mizoram. They face similar limitations to the NHRC - recommendatory powers, limited resources and delays in appointments. Human Rights Courts can also be designated in districts for speedy trial of offences arising from human rights violations (Section 30 of the Act).
The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 provides a legal framework for protection of consumer interests and consumer dispute redressal.

The Consumer Protection Act, 2019, replaced the Consumer Protection Act, 1986, and came into force on 20 July 2020. It defines a 'consumer' as a person who buys goods or hires services for consideration, including online and offline transactions (e-commerce, teleshopping, direct selling), but excludes those who buy for resale or commercial purposes. It recognises six consumer rights: to be protected against hazardous goods and services; to be informed about quality, quantity, potency, purity, standard and price; to be assured of access to goods at competitive prices; to be heard; to seek redressal against unfair or restrictive trade practices; and to consumer awareness.

New features: (1) the Central Consumer Protection Authority (CCPA, 2020) to regulate violations of consumer rights, unfair trade practices and misleading advertisements, with powers to investigate, order recalls, refunds and penalties (including on endorsers of misleading advertisements); (2) product liability - manufacturers, service providers and sellers liable for harm caused by defective products or deficient services; (3) e-filing of complaints and video conferencing for hearings (the e-Daakhil portal); (4) complaints can be filed where the consumer resides or works; (5) mediation as an alternative dispute resolution; (6) penalties for misleading advertisements and adulteration; and (7) the Consumer Protection (E-Commerce) Rules, 2020, regulating online platforms. National Consumer Day is 24 December (the date of the 1986 Act).
Consumer Protection Councils promote and protect consumer rights at different levels under the statutory framework.

Consumer Protection Councils are advisory bodies to promote and protect consumer rights. (1) The Central Consumer Protection Council - chaired by the Union Minister of Consumer Affairs, with other official and non-official members representing consumer interests; meets at least once a year; advises on consumer protection policy. (2) State Consumer Protection Councils - chaired by the state minister in charge of consumer affairs; meet at least twice a year. (3) District Consumer Protection Councils - chaired by the District Collector or Deputy Commissioner; meet at least twice a year.

Their objectives are to promote and protect consumer rights - safety, information, choice, being heard, redressal and education - through awareness, policy advice and coordination among government departments, consumer organisations and businesses. Voluntary consumer organisations (such as the Consumer Guidance Society of India, 1966, and Consumer Education and Research Centre, Ahmedabad) and the 'Jago Grahak Jago' awareness campaign (from 2005) support consumer protection. The National Consumer Helpline (1915) and the e-Daakhil portal help consumers file grievances.
Consumer dispute redressal mechanisms provide institutional forums for adjudicating eligible consumer complaints.

The Act establishes a three-tier quasi-judicial redressal machinery: (1) District Consumer Disputes Redressal Commissions (District Commissions) - presided over by a President (qualified like a district judge) and at least two members; (2) State Consumer Disputes Redressal Commissions; and (3) the National Consumer Disputes Redressal Commission (NCDRC) in New Delhi. Pecuniary jurisdiction (revised by the Consumer Protection (Jurisdiction) Rules, 2021, based on the value of goods or services paid): District Commission up to 50 lakh rupees; State Commission above 50 lakh up to 2 crore rupees; National Commission above 2 crore rupees.

Procedure: complaints can be filed by consumers, voluntary consumer associations, the central or state government, or the CCPA, without the need for a lawyer, with a nominal or no fee; the Commission should decide complaints within three months (five months if testing is required); appeals lie from the District to the State Commission (within 45 days), from the State to the National Commission, and from the National Commission to the Supreme Court. Remedies include removal of defects, replacement, refund, compensation for loss and injury, discontinuance of unfair practices, and punitive damages. Mediation cells are attached to the Commissions. Challenges include delays, vacancies, lack of awareness, and difficulties in enforcing orders.

sections.title: Civil Society, Social Capital and Right to Information

blocks.text:
Civil society consists of voluntary associations and citizen organisations operating outside the direct machinery of the State. It provides space for participation, advocacy and collective action.

Social capital refers to trust, networks and cooperative norms. Civil society can strengthen social capital by creating relationships and habits of participation. In India, civil society organisations have also been important in campaigns for transparency and in using Right to Information mechanisms to hold public authorities accountable.

Civil society: voluntary associations and organisations outside the family, market and state - NGOs, community groups, unions, professional bodies, religious organisations, social movements and media. Origins in political thought - from Aristotle and Cicero, social contract theorists, Ferguson, Hegel, Marx, Tocqueville (associations as schools of democracy), Gramsci (hegemony and counter-hegemony) and Habermas (public sphere), to contemporary revival through democratic movements and development discourse. Functions: representation, advocacy, service delivery, accountability, mobilisation and creating social capital.

Social capital: networks, norms and trust that enable cooperation (Bourdieu, Coleman, Putnam's 'Making Democracy Work' and 'Bowling Alone'); bonding, bridging and linking social capital; benefits for governance, economy and well-being, and risks of exclusion. Civil society and social capital reinforce each other, improving governance and collective action.

Civil society and RTI: the MKSS movement in Rajasthan (jan sunwais from 1994), the NCPRI (1996), state RTI laws and the RTI Act (2005) show how civil society created a powerful tool for transparency and accountability. RTI has been used to expose corruption (such as the Adarsh housing scam), monitor schemes (PDS, MGNREGA) and empower citizens. Challenges include pendency in Information Commissions, attacks on activists, the 2019 amendment, and restrictions on personal information. Civil society remains essential for keeping administration accountable and responsive.

Women's development in the syllabus includes Self Help Groups, gender budgeting and reservation. SHGs can strengthen economic participation, while gender budgeting examines whether public resources respond to women's needs. Reservation seeks greater representation.

The National Policy for Empowerment of Women, 2001 provided a broad policy framework. Child development includes ICDS and ICPS, together with the National Policy for Children, 2013. These measures show how administration addresses welfare, protection and participation of women and children.

Women's development: SHGs (NABARD SHG-Bank Linkage 1992, DAY-NRLM 2011, Kudumbashree) improve savings, credit, livelihoods, confidence and collective action; gender budgeting (since 2005-2006) analyses budgets for their impact on women and allocates resources for gender equality; reservation in local bodies (one-third, increased to 50 percent in many states) and legislatures (106th Amendment, 2023) improves representation. The National Policy for Empowerment of Women (2001) provided goals and strategies for economic, social and political empowerment, legal reforms, gender mainstreaming and the elimination of violence.

Child development: ICDS (1975), now under Mission Saksham Anganwadi and Poshan 2.0, provides nutrition, pre-school education, health check-ups, immunisation and referral services through anganwadis; ICPS (2009), now part of Mission Vatsalya, builds a child protection system through JJBs, CWCs, District Child Protection Units, institutional and non-institutional care, CHILDLINE and adoption; the National Policy for Children (2013) adopts a rights-based approach with priorities of survival, health and nutrition, education, protection and participation.

Evaluation: these measures show how administration addresses the welfare, protection and participation of women and children, combining legal rights, schemes and institutions. Challenges include malnutrition, gender-based violence, low female labour force participation (though rising in recent surveys), proxy representation, inadequate infrastructure and staff, and weak implementation. Civil society, women's organisations (such as the MHIP in Mizoram) and community participation are essential for success.

Human rights protect the dignity and freedom of individuals. The Universal Declaration of Human Rights provides an important international statement of rights.

In India, the National Human Rights Commission and State Human Rights Commissions are institutions concerned with promotion and protection of human rights under the legal framework. Human-rights administration links legal protection with institutional accountability.

Human rights: universal, inalienable and indivisible rights based on dignity; the UDHR (1948) - drafted under Eleanor Roosevelt, 30 articles, foundation of international human rights law; the ICCPR and ICESCR (1966) and specialised conventions. In India, constitutional rights, laws and the judiciary protect human rights, supplemented by statutory institutions.

NHRC (1993): composition headed by a former CJI or Supreme Court judge, members and ex officio chairpersons of national commissions; appointment by a high-level committee; functions - inquiries, court intervention, prison visits, review of laws, research, awareness and NGO support; civil court powers but recommendatory authority. SHRCs: headed by former High Court Chief Justices or judges; appointed by the Governor on a committee's recommendation; inquiry into violations in state subjects; prison visits and awareness. Human Rights Courts in districts.

Evaluation: human rights commissions have raised awareness, issued guidelines (on custodial deaths, encounters, bonded labour), awarded compensation and highlighted issues of marginalised groups. Limitations: non-binding recommendations, time limits, restrictions on investigating armed forces, inadequate staff and funds, delays in appointments and dependence on government. Strengthening their independence and enforcement powers, and cooperation with civil society, would improve human rights administration.

The Consumer Protection Act, 2019 provides a framework for safeguarding consumer interests. Consumer Protection Councils promote consumer rights, while dispute-redressal mechanisms provide forums for eligible consumer complaints.

Consumer administration is important because consumers may face unequal information, unfair practices and defective goods or services. Legal and institutional mechanisms seek accessible remedies and greater accountability.

Need for consumer protection: consumers face information asymmetry, unfair trade practices, defective goods, deficient services, misleading advertisements, adulteration, overcharging and new risks in e-commerce; individual consumers have less power than businesses. The Consumer Protection Act, 2019, replaced the 1986 Act: six consumer rights; coverage of online and offline transactions; the Central Consumer Protection Authority to regulate unfair practices and misleading advertisements; product liability; e-filing (e-Daakhil) and complaints where the consumer resides; mediation; and e-commerce rules.

Consumer Protection Councils: Central (chaired by the Union Minister), State (chaired by the state minister) and District (chaired by the DC) - advisory bodies promoting consumer rights. Redressal: District Commissions (up to 50 lakh rupees), State Commissions (50 lakh to 2 crore) and the National Commission (above 2 crore), with appeals to the Supreme Court; simple procedures, time limits and remedies including refunds, replacement, compensation and punitive damages. Awareness campaigns (Jago Grahak Jago), the National Consumer Helpline (1915) and consumer organisations support the system.

Evaluation: the consumer protection framework provides accessible, inexpensive and quick remedies, and the 2019 Act adapted it to the digital economy. Challenges: low awareness, especially in rural areas, delays and vacancies in Commissions, weak enforcement of orders, and the need for more consumer education and stronger standards (BIS, FSSAI). Consumer protection reflects the principle of citizen-centred administration and accountability of businesses.
Police administration concerns the organisation and management of the police system for maintenance of public order, prevention and investigation of crime and enforcement of law.

Police administration is the organisation, management and functioning of the police force - recruitment, training, deployment, operations, supervision, discipline, welfare and accountability - to maintain public order, prevent and detect crime, enforce laws and protect citizens' rights. In India, 'police' and 'public order' are State subjects (Entries 1 and 2 of List II), so states organise their own police forces, while the Union maintains central armed police forces (CRPF, BSF, CISF, ITBP, SSB, Assam Rifles) and central agencies (CBI, IB, NIA, NCB) under the Ministry of Home Affairs.

The colonial Police Act, 1861 (enacted after the 1857 revolt), still forms the basis of policing in many states, though several states (including Mizoram, Kerala, Bihar and others) have enacted new police acts in line with the Model Police Act (2006, drafted by the Soli Sorabjee Committee) and Supreme Court directions. The new criminal laws - the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, Bharatiya Nagarik Suraksha Sanhita and Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (2023, in force from 1 July 2024) - replaced the IPC, CrPC and Indian Evidence Act and affect police procedures.
Police are an important part of public administration because they protect life and property, maintain order and support the rule of law.

Importance: police are the most visible face of government and the first point of contact for citizens seeking justice. They maintain law and order and public peace; prevent and detect crime; investigate offences and help in prosecution; protect life, property and the rights of citizens, especially vulnerable groups (women, children, SCs and STs, senior citizens); control traffic; manage crowds at events and festivals; provide security for VIPs and vital installations; gather intelligence; respond to disasters and emergencies; counter terrorism and insurgency; and enforce social legislation.

Effective policing is essential for the rule of law, economic development, investment and citizens' sense of security. India's police-population ratio is low (about 150-155 police per lakh population against the UN-suggested 222), with large vacancies, which affects police effectiveness. Police misuse or failure can seriously damage public trust and democracy.
Police organisation generally follows territorial and functional arrangements with defined ranks, authority and specialised units.

State police organisation: headed by the Director General of Police (DGP), assisted by Additional DGPs and Inspectors General of Police (IGPs) in charge of ranges or zones (groups of districts) and specialised branches (crime, intelligence, armed police, training, traffic, CID). Deputy Inspectors General (DIGs) supervise ranges. At the district level, the Superintendent of Police (SP) is the head, assisted by Additional SPs and Deputy SPs or Assistant SPs (in charge of sub-divisions). Police stations are headed by Inspectors or Sub-Inspectors (Station House Officers), with Assistant Sub-Inspectors, Head Constables and Constables. In metropolitan cities, the Commissionerate system gives the Police Commissioner magisterial powers.

Functional units include the armed police (battalions), crime branch and CID, special branch (intelligence), traffic police, women's cells and all-women police stations, cyber crime units, anti-terrorist squads, and the Railway Police. IPS officers (an All-India Service) hold senior posts, while state police service officers and constables form the bulk. Mizoram Police is headed by a DGP, with district SPs, armed battalions (Mizoram Armed Police and India Reserve Battalions), and specialised units such as the anti-narcotics wing; the Assam Rifles and BSF guard the borders.
Maintenance of law and order involves prevention and control of disturbances and protection of public peace under law.

Maintenance of law and order includes preventing and controlling riots, communal and ethnic violence, mob violence, agitations, strikes, demonstrations and other disturbances; ensuring peaceful conduct of elections, festivals and public events; patrolling; intelligence gathering; preventive measures such as orders prohibiting assembly (Section 163 of the BNSS, earlier Section 144 CrPC), preventive detention under special laws, and binding over; and the use of force when necessary, according to law and principles of minimum force.

The District Magistrate (Deputy Commissioner in Mizoram) and the Superintendent of Police share responsibility for law and order in the district (the dual control system), except in Commissionerate areas. Problems: politicisation, communal bias, excessive use of force, inadequate training in crowd control, and lack of non-lethal equipment. Reforms emphasise professional crowd management, intelligence-led policing, community engagement and respect for the right to peaceful protest.
Crime prevention includes measures intended to reduce opportunities and conditions for crime.

Crime prevention measures: (1) patrolling and beat policing to deter crime; (2) surveillance of habitual offenders and history-sheeters; (3) intelligence gathering; (4) situational crime prevention - reducing opportunities through street lighting, CCTV cameras, security systems and urban design (the 'broken windows' theory of James Q. Wilson and George Kelling, 1982, argued that addressing minor disorder prevents serious crime); (5) social crime prevention - addressing root causes such as poverty, unemployment, drug abuse and lack of education through welfare and youth programmes; (6) community policing and neighbourhood watch; (7) awareness campaigns (cyber safety, women's safety, drug abuse); and (8) legal measures (preventive detention, externment).

Technology plays a growing role - the Crime and Criminal Tracking Network and Systems (CCTNS, 2009), facial recognition, predictive policing and emergency response systems (Dial 112). In Mizoram, police work with civil society organisations (the YMA and others) and Village Councils in crime prevention, especially against drug trafficking.
Investigation involves lawful collection and examination of evidence relating to alleged offences.

Investigation is the process of collecting evidence about an offence to identify the offender and prepare the case for trial. Under criminal procedure (now the BNSS, 2023), steps include: registration of the First Information Report (FIR) for cognizable offences (zero FIR and e-FIR are allowed); visiting the scene of crime; collecting physical and forensic evidence; examining witnesses and recording statements; arrest of suspects (with safeguards laid down in D. K. Basu v. State of West Bengal, 1997 - arrest memo, informing relatives, medical examination); searches and seizures; interrogation; obtaining expert opinions; and filing the charge sheet (final report) in court. The BNSS requires videography of searches and forensic investigation for offences punishable with seven years or more.

Problems: overburdened police, lack of separation of investigation from law and order duties, inadequate forensic facilities and training, use of third-degree methods and custodial violence, political interference, delays, low conviction rates and poor coordination with prosecutors. Reforms: separate investigation wings (as directed in Prakash Singh, 2006), forensic science laboratories and the National Forensic Sciences University (2020), training in scientific investigation and cyber crime, and better witness protection (Witness Protection Scheme, 2018).
Effective policing requires public trust, communication and cooperation. Poor relations can reduce reporting and weaken legitimacy.

Good police-public relations are essential because police depend on the public for information, reporting crimes, witnesses and cooperation. In India, public perception of police is often negative due to corruption, rude behaviour, refusal to register FIRs, custodial violence, political bias and delays. The poor, women, Dalits and minorities often face discrimination.

Measures to improve relations: courteous and responsive behaviour; easy registration of complaints (e-FIRs, help desks, women's help desks in police stations); transparency and timely information to complainants; citizen charters; public grievance redressal; community policing; police-public meetings and friendly police initiatives; outreach to students and youth; training in soft skills, human rights and gender sensitivity; use of social media for communication; and visible accountability for misconduct. Positive examples include Kerala's Janamaithri Suraksha (2008) and Tamil Nadu's Friends of Police (1993).
Police accountability means that police powers must be exercised according to law and remain subject to institutional and public oversight.

Police accountability mechanisms: (1) internal - hierarchy, supervision, departmental inquiries and discipline; (2) political - control by the state government and the Home Department (which can also lead to misuse); (3) legislative - questions and debates in legislatures; (4) judicial - courts can review police actions, issue writs (habeas corpus), award compensation for custodial violence (Nilabati Behera, 1993) and lay down guidelines (D. K. Basu, 1997; Lalita Kumari, 2014, making FIR registration mandatory for cognizable offences); (5) independent bodies - the NHRC and SHRCs, Police Complaints Authorities at state and district levels (directed in Prakash Singh, 2006) to inquire into serious misconduct (custodial death, rape, grievous hurt); and (6) public accountability - media, civil society, RTI and body cameras and CCTV in police stations (Paramvir Singh Saini, 2020).

Accountability is needed because police have powers of arrest, detention, use of force and investigation that can be abused. Balancing operational autonomy (freedom from political interference) with accountability (to law and the public) is the central challenge of police reform.
Police reforms seek improvements in professionalism, training, accountability, investigation, working conditions and public service.

Commissions and committees: the National Police Commission (Dharma Vira, 1977-1981, eight reports), the Ribeiro Committee (1998), the Padmanabhaiah Committee (2000), the Malimath Committee on criminal justice reforms (2003), the Model Police Act drafting committee (Soli Sorabjee, 2006) and the Second ARC (5th report, 'Public Order', 2007). In Prakash Singh v. Union of India (2006), the Supreme Court issued seven directives: (1) a State Security Commission to lay down broad policy and evaluate performance, insulating the police from political pressure; (2) selection of the DGP from among the three senior-most officers empanelled by the UPSC, with a minimum tenure of two years; (3) minimum two-year tenure for IGPs, DIGs, SPs and SHOs; (4) separation of investigation and law and order functions in larger cities; (5) a Police Establishment Board to decide transfers, postings and promotions of officers of DSP rank and below; (6) Police Complaints Authorities at state and district levels; and (7) a National Security Commission for central police organisations.

Other reform needs: filling vacancies and improving the police-population ratio; better pay, housing and working conditions (long hours, lack of leave); modernisation (weapons, vehicles, communication, forensics, CCTNS); training in human rights, gender sensitivity and cyber crime; increasing women's representation (about 11-12 percent of police personnel); community policing; and enacting new police laws. Implementation of the Prakash Singh directions by states has been partial and slow.
Community policing encourages cooperation between police and local communities to identify and address safety problems.

Community policing is a philosophy and strategy in which the police and the community work together as partners to identify and solve problems of crime, disorder and fear, building trust and legitimacy. Elements: decentralised policing (beat officers responsible for specific areas), regular interaction with residents, problem-solving rather than only reacting to incidents (Herman Goldstein's problem-oriented policing), and community participation in decisions on local safety priorities. It developed in the USA, the UK (neighbourhood policing) and Japan (koban system of neighbourhood police boxes).

Indian examples: Kerala's Janamaithri Suraksha Project (2008), with beat officers visiting households and community committees; Tamil Nadu's Friends of Police; Mumbai's Mohalla Committees (after the 1992-1993 riots) for communal harmony; Delhi's Neighbourhood Watch Scheme; Hyderabad's community CCTV initiatives; and in Mizoram, cooperation between police, Village Councils, Local Councils and civil society organisations such as the YMA, particularly in anti-drug campaigns and maintaining order. Benefits: improved trust, better information and crime prevention, reduced fear, and more accountable policing. Challenges: police resistance, lack of resources and training, frequent transfers, and the risk of vigilantism or exclusion of minorities.

sections.title: Meaning, Nature and Importance of Police Administration

blocks.text:
Police administration is the organisation and management of policing for maintenance of public order and enforcement of law. Police protect life and property, prevent crime and support lawful investigation.

Because police possess significant coercive powers, their administration must combine operational effectiveness with legality, discipline and accountability. Professional policing is therefore an essential part of democratic public administration.

Meaning and nature: police administration involves organising and managing the police force for maintaining order, preventing and investigating crime and enforcing law; police is a State subject, with central forces and agencies under the Ministry of Home Affairs; the Police Act, 1861, still governs many states, while new state laws and the 2023 criminal laws are changing the framework. Policing combines coercive authority with service functions.

Importance: police maintain law and order, protect life, property and rights, investigate crimes, ensure security, respond to emergencies, and enforce social legislation; they are the most visible face of government. The low police-population ratio, vacancies and heavy workload affect effectiveness.

Democratic policing: because police have significant coercive powers, their administration must ensure legality (respect for law and procedures), professionalism (training, skills, ethics), impartiality (no bias on grounds of religion, caste or politics), accountability (internal, judicial, independent and public) and responsiveness to citizens. As the National Police Commission noted, police must be a service, not only a force. Professional and accountable policing is essential for the rule of law and democracy.

Police organisations use defined ranks, territorial jurisdictions and specialised units. Their main functions include maintenance of law and order, prevention of crime and investigation of offences.

These functions require trained personnel, coordination, records, intelligence and lawful procedures. Effective administration also requires clear command structures and adequate resources.

Organisation: the DGP heads the state police, with ADGPs, IGPs and DIGs for zones, ranges and specialised branches; the SP heads the district, with Additional SPs, DSPs and SHOs at police stations, down to constables; commissionerates in metropolitan cities; specialised units - armed police, CID and crime branch, intelligence, traffic, women's cells, cyber cells, anti-terrorism and anti-narcotics units; central forces (CRPF, BSF, CISF, ITBP, SSB, Assam Rifles) and agencies (CBI, IB, NIA, NCB). Mizoram Police includes district police, armed battalions and specialised units, with the Assam Rifles and BSF guarding international borders.

Functions: law and order (preventing and controlling disturbances, crowd management, preventive measures), crime prevention (patrolling, surveillance, situational and social prevention, technology), crime investigation (FIR, evidence collection, arrest with safeguards, forensic investigation, charge sheet), traffic management, security, intelligence, disaster response and social legislation enforcement. The District Magistrate and SP coordinate law and order in districts.

Requirements: trained and adequate personnel, clear command structure, coordination among units and with other agencies (prosecution, courts, forensic labs, prisons), modern equipment and technology (CCTNS, forensic labs, communication), records and data, and lawful procedures. Problems include vacancies, poor working conditions, inadequate training, outdated laws and political interference.

Police depend on public cooperation for information, crime reporting and community safety. Trust, fairness and respectful treatment therefore improve police effectiveness and legitimacy.

Accountability ensures that police authority is exercised within law. Oversight, disciplinary mechanisms and transparent procedures are important because misuse of police power can damage public confidence.

Police-public relations: cooperation of the public is essential for information and crime reporting; negative perceptions arise from corruption, misbehaviour, refusal to register FIRs, custodial violence and bias. Improvement measures include courtesy and responsiveness, help desks, e-FIRs, citizen charters, grievance redressal, transparency, community outreach, training in soft skills, human rights and gender sensitivity, social media communication, and examples such as Janamaithri and Friends of Police.

Accountability: internal supervision and discipline; government control; legislative oversight; judicial review and guidelines (D. K. Basu 1997 on arrest, Nilabati Behera 1993 on compensation, Lalita Kumari 2014 on FIR, Paramvir Singh Saini 2020 on CCTV); NHRC and SHRCs; Police Complaints Authorities (Prakash Singh 2006); and media, civil society and RTI. Custodial deaths, fake encounters and misuse of laws show why accountability is essential.

Balance: police need operational autonomy from political interference to function professionally, but must remain accountable to law and the public. Trust, fairness and respectful treatment improve police legitimacy and effectiveness, while misuse of power damages public confidence. Democratic policing requires both effectiveness and accountability.

Police reform aims to improve professionalism, training, investigation, accountability, technology and service conditions. Reform also seeks a more citizen-oriented police system.

Community policing promotes partnership between police and communities. It encourages local cooperation and problem-solving rather than relying only on reactive enforcement.

Police reforms: the National Police Commission (1977-1981), Ribeiro, Padmanabhaiah, Malimath and Sorabjee committees, the Second ARC, and the Prakash Singh judgement (2006) with seven directives - State Security Commission, DGP selection and tenure, fixed tenure for key officers, separation of investigation and law and order, Police Establishment Board, Police Complaints Authority and National Security Commission. Other reform areas: filling vacancies, better working conditions, modernisation, forensic capacity, training, more women in the police, new police acts, and implementation of the 2023 criminal laws. Implementation by states has been slow and partial.

Community policing: partnership between police and community for problem-solving; elements - beat policing, regular interaction, community committees, problem-oriented policing; examples - Japan's koban, Kerala's Janamaithri, Tamil Nadu's Friends of Police, Mumbai's Mohalla Committees and Delhi's Neighbourhood Watch; in Mizoram, cooperation with Village Councils and civil society. Benefits - trust, information, crime prevention, reduced fear and accountability; challenges - resistance, resources, transfers and the risk of vigilantism.

Conclusion: reforms aim to transform the colonial-era police into a professional, accountable, citizen-friendly service. Technology (CCTNS, forensic labs, emergency response, body cameras) and community policing complement structural reforms. Without political will to implement reforms and insulate the police from improper interference, improvements remain limited.

sections.title: PUB 305 – TRIBAL DEVELOPMENT ADMINISTRATION IN INDIA
SHORT NOTES
context: PUB 305 – TRIBAL DEVELOPMENT ADMINISTRATION IN INDIA

sections.title: Tribal Development Administration
context: PUB 305 – TRIBAL DEVELOPMENT ADMINISTRATION IN INDIA

blocks.text: Tribal development administration refers to policies, institutions and programmes designed for the social, economic and administrative development of Scheduled Tribes.

Scheduled Tribes are communities notified by the President under Article 342 (for each state or UT), based on criteria such as primitive traits, distinctive culture, geographical isolation, shyness of contact with the community at large and backwardness (the Lokur Committee, 1965). There are over 700 Scheduled Tribes, forming about 8.6 percent of India's population (10.4 crore in the 2011 Census); 75 groups are classified as Particularly Vulnerable Tribal Groups (PVTGs). Mizoram, Lakshadweep, Nagaland and Meghalaya have tribal majorities (over 85 percent); in Mizoram, about 94 percent of the population is ST.

Tribal development administration includes the Ministry of Tribal Affairs (1999), state tribal welfare departments, the National Commission for Scheduled Tribes (2004), Integrated Tribal Development Projects (ITDPs), the Tribal Sub-Plan (now the Development Action Plan for STs), tribal research institutes, TRIFED (1987) and NSTFDC (2001), and Fifth and Sixth Schedule institutions. Approaches include isolation (Verrier Elwin's earlier 'national park' approach), assimilation, and integration (Nehru's 'Panchsheel for tribal development', 1958, which stressed development along the lines of their own genius, respect for tribal rights in land and forests, training tribal people for administration, avoiding over-administration and judging results by quality of life rather than money spent).

sections.title: Need for Tribal Development
context: PUB 305 – TRIBAL DEVELOPMENT ADMINISTRATION IN INDIA

blocks.text: Tribal development seeks to address deprivation while protecting cultural identity, land, livelihood and constitutional safeguards.

Need: Scheduled Tribes face poverty (in 2011-2012, about 45 percent of STs in rural areas lived below the poverty line, compared with about 26 percent nationally), low literacy (59 percent in 2011 versus 73 percent overall, though Mizoram's tribal literacy is very high), poor health outcomes (malnutrition, high infant mortality, sickle cell anaemia), lack of infrastructure in remote and forest areas, land alienation and displacement by dams, mines and industrial projects (tribals constitute a large share of those displaced by development projects), exploitation by moneylenders and traders, loss of forest rights, unemployment and migration, and in some areas, insurgency (Left-wing extremism in central India).

Development must balance improving living standards, education, health, livelihoods and access to services with protecting tribal identity, culture, languages, land, forests and self-governance. The Xaxa Committee (2014) on the socio-economic, health and educational status of tribal communities highlighted persistent deprivation and recommended stronger implementation of protective laws (PESA, FRA) and participatory development.

sections.title: Constitutional Safeguards
context: PUB 305 – TRIBAL DEVELOPMENT ADMINISTRATION IN INDIA

blocks.text: The Constitution provides special safeguards and provisions for Scheduled Tribes, including protective, developmental and representational measures.

Constitutional safeguards for STs: (1) protective - Article 15(4) (special provisions for advancement), Article 16(4) and 16(4A) (reservation in jobs and promotions), Article 19(5) (restrictions on free movement and residence in tribal areas to protect them), Article 23 (against forced labour), Article 29 (protection of culture and language), Article 46 (promotion of educational and economic interests and protection from social injustice and exploitation), Article 164(1) (a tribal welfare minister in Chhattisgarh, Jharkhand, Madhya Pradesh and Odisha), Article 244 (administration of Scheduled and tribal areas - Fifth and Sixth Schedules), Article 275(1) (grants for tribal welfare and Scheduled Areas), and Article 339 (Union control over administration of Scheduled Areas and ST welfare); (2) political - reservation of seats in the Lok Sabha (47) and state assemblies (Articles 330, 332), panchayats and municipalities (Articles 243D, 243T), extended until 2030 for legislatures (Article 334); (3) institutional - the National Commission for Scheduled Tribes (Article 338A, 89th Amendment, 2003).

Special provisions for certain states: Article 371A (Nagaland - protection of Naga customary law and ownership of land and resources), 371B (Assam), 371C (Manipur hill areas), 371F (Sikkim), 371G (Mizoram - protection of Mizo religious and social practices, customary law, administration of justice according to customary law, and ownership and transfer of land), and 371H (Arunachal Pradesh). Laws include the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act (1989), PESA (1996) and the Forest Rights Act (2006).

sections.title: Fifth Schedule
context: PUB 305 – TRIBAL DEVELOPMENT ADMINISTRATION IN INDIA

blocks.text: The Fifth Schedule provides a constitutional framework for administration and control of Scheduled Areas and Scheduled Tribes in specified parts of India.

The Fifth Schedule (Article 244(1)) applies to Scheduled Areas in states other than Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram. Ten states have Scheduled Areas: Andhra Pradesh, Telangana, Chhattisgarh, Gujarat, Himachal Pradesh, Jharkhand, Madhya Pradesh, Maharashtra, Odisha and Rajasthan. The President declares Scheduled Areas (based on criteria such as preponderance of tribal population, compactness, under-developed nature and economic disparity) and can alter them in consultation with the Governor.

Provisions: the executive power of the state extends to Scheduled Areas, but the Governor has special responsibilities - submitting an annual report to the President on the administration of Scheduled Areas; directing that any Act of Parliament or the state legislature shall not apply or shall apply with modifications; and making regulations for peace and good government, particularly to prohibit or restrict transfer of land by or among STs, regulate allotment of land, and regulate moneylending to STs (after consulting the Tribes Advisory Council). The Union can give directions to states on administration of Scheduled Areas. A Tribes Advisory Council is required in each state with Scheduled Areas. The PESA Act (Panchayats (Extension to Scheduled Areas) Act, 1996), based on the Bhuria Committee (1995), extends panchayats to Fifth Schedule areas with special powers for gram sabhas over natural resources, minor forest produce, land alienation, moneylending and social customs. Implementation of PESA has been weak in many states.

sections.title: Sixth Schedule
context: PUB 305 – TRIBAL DEVELOPMENT ADMINISTRATION IN INDIA

blocks.text: The Sixth Schedule provides autonomous administrative arrangements for certain tribal areas of Northeast India through Autonomous District and Regional Councils.

The Sixth Schedule (Articles 244(2) and 275(1)) applies to tribal areas of Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram, based on the Bordoloi Sub-Committee's recommendations.
