It provides for Autonomous District Councils (and Regional Councils) with elected members (up to 30, including up to four nominated by the Governor), with legislative powers over land, forests, jhum, water, village and town administration, inheritance, marriage, divorce and social customs; judicial powers through village and district courts applying customary law; and powers to levy taxes and manage primary education, health, markets and roads.

There are ten ADCs: in Assam - the Bodoland Territorial Council, Karbi Anglong ADC and Dima Hasao ADC; in Meghalaya - Khasi Hills, Jaintia Hills and Garo Hills ADCs; in Tripura - the Tripura Tribal Areas ADC; and in Mizoram - the Chakma, Lai and Mara ADCs. The Sixth Schedule provides more autonomy than the Fifth Schedule. Issues: financial dependence on state governments, overlapping powers, political conflicts, irregular elections, and demands for greater powers (the Constitution (125th Amendment) Bill, 2019, proposed more powers and funds). Demands for Sixth Schedule status have also come from other areas, such as Ladakh (2023-2025 protests).

sections.title: Tribal Advisory Council
context: PUB 305 – TRIBAL DEVELOPMENT ADMINISTRATION IN INDIA

blocks.text: Tribal Advisory Councils are constitutional institutions associated with Scheduled Areas under the Fifth Schedule and advise on matters concerning tribal welfare and advancement.

Under paragraph 4 of the Fifth Schedule, every state with Scheduled Areas must establish a Tribes Advisory Council (TAC); the President may also direct states with STs but no Scheduled Areas (such as Tamil Nadu and West Bengal) to set up TACs. A TAC has not more than 20 members, of whom about three-fourths should be ST members of the state Legislative Assembly (if there are fewer ST MLAs, remaining seats are filled by other STs). It is usually chaired by the Chief Minister or the Tribal Welfare Minister.

Functions: advising on matters relating to the welfare and advancement of STs in the state that are referred to it by the Governor - such as regulations on land transfer and moneylending, development programmes, and the application of laws to Scheduled Areas. The Governor must consult the TAC before making regulations under paragraph 5. Criticisms: TACs meet infrequently, have only advisory powers, are dominated by the state government, and have not effectively protected tribal interests; there have been disputes over whether the Governor or the Chief Minister should control TAC appointments (for example, in Jharkhand in 2021).

sections.title: Autonomous District Councils
context: PUB 305 – TRIBAL DEVELOPMENT ADMINISTRATION IN INDIA

blocks.text: ADCs under the Sixth Schedule exercise specified legislative, administrative, judicial and financial powers according to the constitutional framework.

ADCs under the Sixth Schedule exercise: (1) legislative powers (paragraph 3) - laws on land allotment and use (except reserved forests), forest management, water use, jhum cultivation, village and town committees and administration (including police and public health), appointment and succession of chiefs or headmen, inheritance, marriage, divorce and social customs - subject to the Governor's assent; (2) judicial powers (paragraphs 4-5) - village councils and district council courts to try suits and cases between STs according to customary law, with appeals to the High Court; serious criminal cases are excluded; (3) executive and administrative powers (paragraph 6) - establishing and managing primary schools, dispensaries, markets, cattle pounds, ferries, fisheries, roads, road transport and waterways; (4) financial powers (paragraphs 7-8) - a District Fund, land revenue, taxes on professions, trades, animals, vehicles, entry of goods into markets, tolls, and receiving grants from the state; and (5) regulatory powers (paragraph 10) - regulating moneylending and trading by non-tribals.

The Governor plays a key role - creating councils, determining their areas, appointing commissions of inquiry, applying or modifying laws, and suspending or dissolving councils. In Mizoram, the Lai, Mara and Chakma ADCs function with these powers, supported by funds from the state government.

sections.title: Tribal Development Programmes
context: PUB 305 – TRIBAL DEVELOPMENT ADMINISTRATION IN INDIA

blocks.text: Development programmes seek improvement in education, health, livelihoods, infrastructure and economic opportunities among tribal communities.

Major programmes and schemes for tribal development: (1) planning strategies - the Tribal Sub-Plan (TSP, introduced in the Fifth Five-Year Plan, 1974-1975), requiring states and central ministries to allocate funds in proportion to the ST population (now called the Scheduled Tribe Component or Development Action Plan for STs); (2) education - Eklavya Model Residential Schools (1997-1998, expanded to over 700 schools), pre-matric and post-matric scholarships, ashram schools and hostels, and National Fellowships; (3) livelihoods - Van Dhan Vikas Kendras (2018) for value addition to minor forest produce, Minimum Support Price for Minor Forest Produce (2013), TRIFED's marketing of tribal products, NSTFDC loans and the Pradhan Mantri Van Dhan Yojana; (4) health - programmes for sickle cell anaemia (National Sickle Cell Anaemia Elimination Mission, 2023) and tribal health under the National Health Mission; and (5) infrastructure - roads, electrification, drinking water and housing under general and special schemes.

Recent initiatives: the Pradhan Mantri Janjatiya Adivasi Nyaya Maha Abhiyan (PM-JANMAN, 2023) for PVTGs, providing housing, roads, water, health, education and livelihoods; the Pradhan Mantri Adi Adarsh Gram Yojana (2021) for villages with significant tribal populations; the Dharti Aaba Janjatiya Gram Utkarsh Abhiyan (2024) for saturating basic services in tribal villages; Janjatiya Gaurav Divas (15 November, Birsa Munda's birth anniversary, since 2021); and implementation of the Forest Rights Act (2006), recognising individual and community forest rights (over 20 lakh claims approved).

sections.title: Tribal Development Agencies
context: PUB 305 – TRIBAL DEVELOPMENT ADMINISTRATION IN INDIA

blocks.text: Special institutions and administrative arrangements are used to plan, coordinate and implement tribal development programmes.

Integrated Tribal Development Projects or Agencies (ITDPs or ITDAs) were set up from 1974-1975 in areas with tribal concentration (about 50 percent tribal population in blocks) to plan and implement development programmes in an integrated way under the Tribal Sub-Plan; there are about 190-200 ITDPs, headed by a Project Officer or Project Administrator. Modified Area Development Approach (MADA) pockets and clusters cover smaller tribal concentrations, and micro projects target PVTGs.

Other institutions: the Ministry of Tribal Affairs (1999); state tribal welfare departments; Tribal Research Institutes (in states, for research, evaluation and training); TRIFED (Tribal Cooperative Marketing Development Federation of India, 1987) for marketing tribal products and minor forest produce; the National Scheduled Tribes Finance and Development Corporation (NSTFDC, 2001) for concessional loans; state tribal development corporations; the National Commission for Scheduled Tribes (2004) for monitoring safeguards; and Sixth Schedule ADCs and PESA gram sabhas for local self-governance. In Mizoram, as a tribal-majority state, tribal development is largely mainstreamed through state departments, with ADCs in the south and central schemes implemented by line departments.

sections.title: Problems of Tribal Development
context: PUB 305 – TRIBAL DEVELOPMENT ADMINISTRATION IN INDIA

blocks.text: Major issues may include poverty, remoteness, weak infrastructure, land alienation, limited access to services and the challenge of balancing development with cultural protection.

Problems: (1) land alienation - transfer of tribal land to non-tribals through fraud, moneylenders, encroachment and acquisition for projects, despite protective laws; (2) displacement by dams (Sardar Sarovar, Polavaram), mining (Odisha, Jharkhand, Chhattisgarh), industries and protected areas, often with inadequate rehabilitation; (3) restrictions on forest rights and livelihoods, and slow implementation of the Forest Rights Act; (4) poverty, indebtedness and exploitation by middlemen; (5) poor health and nutrition, and lack of healthcare access in remote areas; (6) low quality of education, high dropout rates, and the language barrier when education is not in tribal languages; (7) inadequate infrastructure - roads, electricity, communication; (8) weak implementation of PESA and TSP funds diverted or under-utilised; (9) cultural erosion and loss of identity due to assimilation and migration; (10) Left-wing extremism in some tribal areas and its security response; and (11) inadequate representation in decision-making.

Solutions recommended by committees (Dhebar Commission 1960-1961, Bhuria Committee 1995, Xaxa Committee 2014): effective implementation of protective laws, participatory planning with gram sabhas, culturally sensitive education in mother tongues, improved health services, livelihood support based on forests and agriculture, fair compensation and rehabilitation, accountable use of funds, and empowering tribal self-governance institutions. Development must be with the consent and participation of tribal communities ('development without destruction').

sections.title: Meaning and Need of Tribal Development Administration
context: PUB 305 – TRIBAL DEVELOPMENT ADMINISTRATION IN INDIA

blocks.text:
Tribal development administration is concerned with public policies and institutions for the development and protection of Scheduled Tribes. Its purpose is not only economic growth but also access to education, health, livelihoods and public services while respecting tribal identity and rights.

Special administrative attention is required because many tribal communities face geographical isolation, infrastructure gaps and historical disadvantage.

Meaning: tribal development administration comprises policies, institutions and programmes for the social, economic, educational and political development of Scheduled Tribes, while protecting their identity, land, forests, culture and rights. Scheduled Tribes (Article 342) include over 700 groups (8.6 percent of the population) and 75 PVTGs; Mizoram is a tribal-majority state.

Approaches: isolation (Elwin's early view), assimilation, and integration with respect for tribal culture (Nehru's Panchsheel for tribal development, 1958). Institutions: the Ministry of Tribal Affairs, state departments, NCST, ITDPs, TRIFED, NSTFDC, Tribal Research Institutes, and Fifth and Sixth Schedule bodies.

Need: tribal communities face poverty, low literacy (in many states), poor health, remoteness and lack of infrastructure, land alienation, displacement, loss of forest rights, exploitation and in some regions conflict. Special administrative attention is needed to address historical disadvantage, ensure access to services and opportunities, and protect tribal rights and culture. Development should be participatory and culturally sensitive, respecting the right of tribal communities to determine their own priorities.

sections.title: Constitutional Safeguards for Scheduled Tribes
context: PUB 305 – TRIBAL DEVELOPMENT ADMINISTRATION IN INDIA

blocks.text:
The Constitution provides special arrangements for Scheduled Tribes. These include protective and developmental provisions and special systems of administration in tribal areas.

The Fifth Schedule concerns Scheduled Areas in specified parts of India and includes arrangements such as Tribal Advisory Councils. The Sixth Schedule applies to certain tribal areas of Northeast India and provides autonomous institutions with specified powers.

Protective safeguards: Articles 15(4), 16(4), 16(4A), 19(5), 23, 29, 46, 244, 275(1), 339 and Article 164(1) (tribal welfare ministers). Political safeguards: reservation in the Lok Sabha (47 seats), state assemblies, panchayats and municipalities. Institutional safeguards: the National Commission for Scheduled Tribes (Article 338A). Special provisions for northeastern and other states under Article 371A-H, including Article 371G for Mizoram. Legal safeguards: the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act (1989, amended 2015 and 2018), PESA (1996), the Forest Rights Act (2006), and state laws on land transfer.

Fifth Schedule: Scheduled Areas in ten states; Governor's special responsibilities and regulation-making powers (land transfer, moneylending); Tribes Advisory Councils; Union directions; PESA for local self-government with empowered gram sabhas. Sixth Schedule: tribal areas of Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura and Mizoram; Autonomous District Councils with legislative, judicial, executive and financial powers; protection of customary law and institutions.

Evaluation: constitutional safeguards have provided protection and representation, but implementation is uneven - land alienation, displacement, weak PESA implementation, TACs' limited role, and financial constraints of ADCs remain problems. The Sixth Schedule model is considered more effective in protecting tribal autonomy than the Fifth Schedule, and demands for Sixth Schedule status have arisen in other regions.

sections.title: Fifth and Sixth Schedule Institutions
context: PUB 305 – TRIBAL DEVELOPMENT ADMINISTRATION IN INDIA

blocks.text:
Under the Fifth Schedule, the constitutional framework provides special administration for Scheduled Areas and includes Tribal Advisory Councils. Under the Sixth Schedule, Autonomous District and Regional Councils exercise specified powers.

These arrangements recognise that tribal regions may require institutions adapted to local social and cultural conditions while remaining within the constitutional system.

Fifth Schedule institutions: the Governor (annual report to the President, power to apply or modify laws and make regulations for Scheduled Areas); the Tribes Advisory Council (up to 20 members, three-fourths ST MLAs; advises on tribal welfare and must be consulted on regulations); the Union government (can issue directions); PESA gram sabhas and panchayats (control over land, forests, minor forest produce, minor minerals, moneylending, markets and social customs). Weaknesses: Governors have rarely used their powers; TACs are advisory and inactive; PESA rules were delayed in many states.

Sixth Schedule institutions: Autonomous District and Regional Councils with elected members; legislative powers over land, forests, jhum, village administration, chiefs, inheritance, marriage and customs; judicial powers through customary courts; executive powers over schools, health, markets and roads; financial powers (District Fund, taxes and grants); regulation of moneylending by non-tribals; the Governor's supervisory powers. In Mizoram, the Lai, Mara and Chakma ADCs function under the Sixth Schedule.

Significance: these arrangements recognise that tribal regions need institutions adapted to their social, cultural and historical conditions - customary law, community land ownership and traditional self-governance - while remaining within the constitutional system. They reflect asymmetric federalism and are vital for protecting tribal identity and enabling self-government.

sections.title: Problems and Programmes of Tribal Development
context: PUB 305 – TRIBAL DEVELOPMENT ADMINISTRATION IN INDIA

blocks.text:
Tribal development programmes focus on education, health, livelihoods, infrastructure and economic opportunities. Special agencies and administrative arrangements are needed for planning and implementation.

Challenges include remoteness, poverty, weak connectivity, land issues and limited service access. Development policy must therefore combine material improvement with protection of legitimate cultural and community interests.

Programmes: Tribal Sub-Plan (1974-1975) and Development Action Plans for STs; ITDPs, MADA and micro projects for PVTGs; Eklavya Model Residential Schools, scholarships and hostels; Van Dhan Vikas Kendras, MSP for minor forest produce, TRIFED and NSTFDC; health programmes (sickle cell mission); infrastructure schemes; PM-JANMAN (2023) for PVTGs, PM Adi Adarsh Gram Yojana and the Dharti Aaba Janjatiya Gram Utkarsh Abhiyan (2024); and the Forest Rights Act (2006) recognising individual and community forest rights.

Problems: land alienation, displacement and inadequate rehabilitation, weak implementation of FRA and PESA, poverty and indebtedness, health and nutrition deficits, poor quality education and dropouts, infrastructure gaps, under-utilisation or diversion of TSP funds, cultural erosion, Left-wing extremism and inadequate participation in decision-making.

Way forward: participatory planning through gram sabhas and ADCs; effective enforcement of protective laws; culturally appropriate education in mother tongues; strengthening health systems in tribal areas; forest-based livelihoods and fair markets; fair compensation and consent for projects; accountability for funds; and capacity-building of tribal institutions. Tribal development must combine material improvement with protection of culture, community rights and the environment - 'development with dignity'.
E-Governance is the use of information and communication technologies in government processes, administration and delivery of public services.

E-governance is the use of ICT to improve the efficiency, effectiveness, transparency and accountability of government and the delivery of services to citizens and businesses. UNESCO defines it as 'the public sector's use of information and communication technologies with the aim of improving information and service delivery, encouraging citizen participation in the decision-making process and making government more accountable, transparent and effective'. The Second ARC's 11th report, 'Promoting e-Governance: The SMART Way Forward' (2008), described SMART governance - Simple, Moral, Accountable, Responsive and Transparent.

E-governance differs from e-government: e-government refers to the use of ICT within government (digitising processes), while e-governance is broader, including relationships with citizens, businesses and civil society and participation in governance. Stages (Gartner model): information (websites), interaction (two-way communication, downloading forms), transaction (online services and payments) and transformation (integrated, citizen-centric services).
Its objectives include improving efficiency, accessibility, transparency, responsiveness and quality of public services.

Objectives: (1) better service delivery - convenient, fast, 24x7 access to services from anywhere ('anytime, anywhere'); (2) efficiency - reducing time, cost and paperwork, streamlining processes; (3) transparency - making information and processes visible, reducing discretion; (4) accountability - tracking files and decisions, audit trails; (5) reducing corruption by removing intermediaries and face-to-face contact; (6) citizen participation in policy-making (online consultations, feedback); (7) improved decision-making through data and analytics; (8) inclusion - reaching remote areas and marginalised groups; (9) better coordination among departments; and (10) empowerment of citizens through information.

India's Digital India programme (launched 1 July 2015) has three vision areas: digital infrastructure as a core utility for every citizen; governance and services on demand; and digital empowerment of citizens.
G2C refers to digital interaction and services provided by government directly to citizens.

Government-to-Citizen (G2C) services provide information and services directly to citizens: certificates (birth, death, caste, income, residence), land records (Bhoomi in Karnataka, pioneered in 2001; the Digital India Land Records Modernisation Programme), passports (Passport Seva, 2010), driving licences and vehicle registration (Parivahan), utility bill payments, tax filing (income tax e-filing), scholarships (National Scholarship Portal), pensions, health services (e-Hospital, CoWIN for COVID-19 vaccination, ABHA health IDs under the Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission), education (DIKSHA, SWAYAM), agriculture (PM-KISAN direct transfers, Soil Health Card, e-NAM), grievance redressal (CPGRAMS), RTI online, DigiLocker, the UMANG app and Aadhaar-based services.

Delivery channels include web portals, mobile apps, Common Service Centres (CSCs, over 5 lakh, run by village-level entrepreneurs), kiosks and helplines. In Mizoram, G2C services include online ILP, e-district certificates and other state portals.
G2G refers to electronic communication, information sharing and coordination among government departments and agencies.

Government-to-Government (G2G) involves electronic communication, information sharing, coordination and integration among ministries, departments, states and local bodies. Examples: e-Office (digital file management), the Public Financial Management System (PFMS) for tracking funds, the Integrated Financial Management Systems of states, the Crime and Criminal Tracking Network and Systems (CCTNS), the Interoperable Criminal Justice System (ICJS) linking police, courts, prisons, forensics and prosecution, e-Courts, the GSTN (shared by the Union and states), the National Data Sharing and Accessibility Policy (2012), the PRAGATI platform for project monitoring by the PMO, video conferencing networks, and dashboards for scheme monitoring.

Benefits: faster communication and decision-making, reduced duplication, better coordination, data-driven governance and transparency in fund flows. Challenges: interoperability between different systems, data standards, security, and resistance to sharing data across departments.
G2B covers electronic interaction between government and businesses, such as licences, taxation, procurement and regulatory services.

Government-to-Business (G2B) covers interactions between government and businesses: online company registration and compliance (MCA21 portal of the Ministry of Corporate Affairs), GST registration and returns (GSTN), income tax and TDS filing, customs clearance (ICEGATE, the Single Window Interface for Facilitating Trade - SWIFT), licences and permits through single-window systems (the National Single Window System, 2021; state single windows), e-procurement and public procurement (the Government e-Marketplace - GeM, 2016; the Central Public Procurement Portal), registration of MSMEs (Udyam), environmental clearances (PARIVESH), and labour law compliance (Shram Suvidha portal).

Benefits: ease of doing business (India's ranking in the World Bank's Doing Business report rose from 142nd in 2014 to 63rd in 2019, before the report was discontinued in 2021), reduced corruption and delays in licensing and procurement, transparency in government purchases, and better compliance. Challenges include digital readiness of small businesses, complex procedures and system glitches.
G2E refers to digital services and administrative systems used in government's relationship with its employees.

Government-to-Employee (G2E) refers to digital systems for the relationship between the government and its employees: e-HRMS (electronic Human Resource Management System) for personal records, leave, transfers and service books; payroll and pensions (through PFMS, Bhavishya portal for pension processing, Jeevan Pramaan digital life certificates for pensioners); online performance appraisal (SPARROW for All-India Service officers); training and capacity-building (iGOT Karmayogi platform under Mission Karmayogi); biometric attendance (attendance.gov.in); internal communication and circulars; e-Office; and grievance redressal for employees.

Benefits: efficient personnel management, transparency in transfers and promotions, timely salaries and pensions, reduced paperwork, better training and higher morale. Challenges: digital skills of employees, privacy of employee data, and resistance to monitoring.
E-administration uses digital tools to improve internal government processes, records, communication and management.

E-administration refers to using ICT to improve the internal working of government - digitising records and files, workflow automation, electronic communication, financial management, personnel management, and monitoring systems. In India, e-Office (developed by NIC) enables electronic files, digital signatures, file tracking and knowledge management; by 2024, many central ministries had moved most files to e-Office. Other examples: PFMS, e-HRMS, video conferencing, cloud computing (MeghRaj), and dashboards.

Benefits: faster decision-making, reduced paper and storage, transparency and accountability through audit trails, remote working, and better coordination. Challenges: training staff, changing work culture, cyber security, maintaining digital records over time, and ensuring that old procedures are reformed rather than just digitised ('automating red tape').
E-service delivery provides public services through digital channels to improve convenience and access.

E-service delivery is providing public services to citizens and businesses through digital channels - web portals, mobile apps, kiosks, Common Service Centres, SMS and helplines - instead of or in addition to physical offices. Features: online applications, digital payments (UPI, net banking), document submission through DigiLocker, real-time tracking, time-bound delivery (often linked to Right to Public Services laws), and digital certificates. Direct Benefit Transfer (DBT, 2013), using the JAM trinity (Jan Dhan accounts, Aadhaar and Mobile), transfers subsidies and benefits directly to beneficiaries' bank accounts; the government estimated savings of over 3 lakh crore rupees through DBT by 2023 by eliminating fake and duplicate beneficiaries.

Benefits: convenience, speed, lower cost for citizens, reduced corruption and middlemen, wider reach. Challenges: digital divide, authentication failures (Aadhaar biometric mismatches causing exclusion from rations or pensions), connectivity problems, and the need for assisted access and grievance redressal for those who cannot use digital services.
Digital systems can improve transparency by making information and processes more visible and can strengthen accountability through records and tracking.

E-governance can improve transparency through: proactive disclosure of information on websites (as required by Section 4 of the RTI Act); open data portals (data.gov.in); online tracking of applications and files; e-procurement, which makes tenders and contracts public; real-time dashboards of scheme performance; social audits supported by digital records (MGNREGA's public records of job cards, muster rolls and payments); and geo-tagging of assets (photos with location of houses, toilets and works).

It strengthens accountability through audit trails (who did what and when), time-bound service delivery and monitoring, online grievance redressal (CPGRAMS, state portals), citizen feedback and ratings, and reduced discretion and personal contact, which lowers opportunities for corruption. However, technology alone does not guarantee accountability; it must be supported by institutions, political will and citizens' ability to use information.
The digital divide is inequality in access to devices, connectivity, skills and ability to use digital services.

The digital divide refers to unequal access to and use of digital technologies between groups - by income, location (urban-rural), gender, age, education, disability, language and region. In India, according to surveys, internet use is lower in rural areas, among women (NFHS-5 found that about one-third of women had ever used the internet, compared with over half of men), older people and poorer households. Northeastern and hilly regions face connectivity challenges.

Consequences: exclusion from online services, welfare benefits, education (during COVID-19 online schooling), jobs and information, increasing existing inequalities. Measures: BharatNet (broadband to gram panchayats), PM-WANI (public Wi-Fi), Common Service Centres for assisted access, the Pradhan Mantri Gramin Digital Saksharta Abhiyan (PMGDISHA, 2017, digital literacy for rural citizens), low-cost devices and data, services in regional languages (Bhashini, 2022), accessibility standards for persons with disabilities, and maintaining offline options.
Cybersecurity in e-governance concerns protection of government systems, networks, services and data from digital threats.

Cybersecurity is the protection of computer systems, networks, applications and data from attacks, damage, unauthorised access and disruption. Threats to e-governance include hacking, malware, ransomware (such as the attack on AIIMS New Delhi's servers in November 2022), phishing, denial-of-service attacks, data breaches, insider threats, and state-sponsored cyber attacks on critical infrastructure (such as attempts on the power grid).

India's institutional framework: the Information Technology Act, 2000 (amended 2008) with cyber crime provisions; CERT-In (Indian Computer Emergency Response Team, 2004) as the national agency for cyber incidents, with mandatory reporting of incidents within six hours (2022 directions); the National Critical Information Infrastructure Protection Centre (NCIIPC); the National Cyber Security Policy (2013); the National Cyber Coordination Centre; the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C, 2020) and the cyber crime reporting portal and helpline (1930); and the Digital Personal Data Protection Act (2023). Measures include security audits, encryption, multi-factor authentication, backups, training of personnel and international cooperation.
Privacy concerns the proper collection, use, storage and protection of personal information in digital government.

Digital governance involves collecting large amounts of personal data (Aadhaar biometrics, health records, financial data, location data), raising concerns about surveillance, misuse, data breaches, profiling and lack of consent. In Justice K. S. Puttaswamy v. Union of India (2017), a nine-judge bench of the Supreme Court declared privacy a fundamental right under Article 21; in 2018, it upheld Aadhaar for welfare and PAN linkage but struck down its mandatory use by private companies and for bank accounts and mobile connections.

The Digital Personal Data Protection Act, 2023 (based on the work of the Justice B. N. Srikrishna Committee, 2018) provides for processing of personal data with consent or for legitimate uses; rights of data principals (access, correction, erasure, grievance redressal); duties of data fiduciaries (security safeguards, breach notification); special protections for children's data; a Data Protection Board; and penalties up to 250 crore rupees. Criticisms include broad exemptions for the government and the amendment to the RTI Act restricting disclosure of personal information. The DPDP Rules were notified in 2025. Privacy by design, data minimisation and transparency are essential for trust in e-governance.
Challenges include infrastructure gaps, digital literacy, interoperability, resistance to change, cybersecurity, privacy and unequal access.

Challenges: (1) infrastructure - connectivity, electricity, hardware, especially in rural and hilly areas; (2) digital divide and digital literacy; (3) language barriers - most services in English or Hindi; (4) interoperability - different departments use incompatible systems and data formats; (5) resistance to change from employees and loss of discretionary power; (6) lack of skilled IT personnel in government; (7) cybersecurity threats; (8) privacy and data protection; (9) exclusion errors (biometric authentication failures, network failures); (10) high costs and sustainability of projects; (11) process re-engineering - digitising inefficient procedures without reform; (12) legal and regulatory gaps; (13) inadequate grievance redressal for digital failures; and (14) vendor lock-in and dependence on private contractors.

Solutions: investment in infrastructure (BharatNet), digital literacy programmes, multilingual and accessible services, common standards and interoperable platforms (India Stack), training and change management, strong cybersecurity and data protection, assisted service delivery (CSCs), offline alternatives, citizen feedback and robust monitoring and evaluation.
India has expanded digital public administration through online services, digital platforms and electronic delivery mechanisms across many sectors.

Milestones: the National Informatics Centre (NIC, 1976); computerisation of railway reservations (1986); the Department of Electronics (1970) and the IT Ministry (1999); the IT Act (2000); state initiatives - Bhoomi (Karnataka, land records), FRIENDS (Kerala, bill payments), e-Seva (Andhra Pradesh), Gyandoot (Madhya Pradesh, rural kiosks, 2000); the National e-Governance Plan (NeGP, 2006) with 27 (later 31) Mission Mode Projects (passports, income tax, MCA21, land records, e-courts, e-district, PDS) and the infrastructure of State Wide Area Networks, State Data Centres and Common Service Centres; Aadhaar (UIDAI, 2009); and Digital India (2015).

Digital Public Infrastructure (the 'India Stack'): Aadhaar (over 130 crore enrolments), UPI (2016; over 1,500 crore transactions a month by 2024), DigiLocker, e-Sign, CoWIN, the Account Aggregator framework, ONDC (Open Network for Digital Commerce, 2022), Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission and the GSTN. India promoted its DPI model internationally during the G20 presidency (2023). Rankings: India ranked 105th in the UN E-Government Development Index 2022 and improved to 97th in 2024. In Mizoram, initiatives include the State Data Centre, e-district services, online ILP and e-Office in the secretariat.
E-governance can support good governance when technology improves transparency, participation, efficiency, accountability and citizen-oriented service.

Good governance, as defined by the World Bank (1992) and UNDP (1997), includes participation, rule of law, transparency, responsiveness, consensus orientation, equity and inclusiveness, effectiveness and efficiency, and accountability. E-governance can support these: participation (online consultations - MyGov portal, 2014; e-petitions), transparency (open data, RTI online, e-procurement), accountability (tracking, audit trails, grievance redressal), responsiveness (quick services, feedback), efficiency (reduced time and cost), equity (DBT reducing leakages, reaching remote areas) and rule of law (e-courts, digital records).

However, e-governance supports good governance only when it is citizen-centric, inclusive, secure and accompanied by process reforms and institutional accountability. Without these, it may increase exclusion, surveillance or simply digitise inefficiency. The Second ARC recommended building a climate for e-governance, process re-engineering, capacity-building, protection of critical information infrastructure, and monitoring and evaluation. E-governance is a means to good governance, not an end in itself.

sections.title: Meaning, Objectives and Significance of E-Governance

blocks.text:
E-Governance means applying information and communication technology to governmental processes and public services. Its purpose is not merely computerisation but improvement of administration and interaction with citizens.

Major objectives include efficiency, accessibility, transparency, responsiveness and better service delivery. When properly designed, e-governance can reduce delays, improve records and make public services easier to access.

Meaning: e-governance is the application of ICT to government processes, administration and service delivery - including relationships with citizens, businesses, employees and other governments - to achieve SMART governance (Simple, Moral, Accountable, Responsive, Transparent). It is broader than e-government (internal computerisation) and progresses through stages of information, interaction, transaction and transformation.

Objectives: better and faster service delivery, efficiency and cost reduction, transparency, accountability, reduced corruption, citizen participation, data-driven decision-making, inclusion of remote areas and improved coordination. Significance: in India, e-governance has transformed services - Aadhaar, UPI, DBT, DigiLocker, GeM, CoWIN and e-courts have improved access, reduced leakages and increased transparency.

Evaluation: e-governance is not merely computerisation; it requires rethinking processes from the citizen's perspective, building capacity, ensuring inclusion and security, and integrating services. Successful examples combine technology with institutional reform and political commitment; failures occur when technology is imposed without considering users' needs, infrastructure and digital skills.

E-governance interactions can be classified as Government-to-Citizen, Government-to-Government, Government-to-Business and Government-to-Employee. G2C focuses on public services, G2G on interdepartmental coordination, G2B on regulatory and business interactions and G2E on government personnel.

These models show that digital government affects both internal administration and external relationships.

G2C (Government to Citizen): services for citizens - certificates, land records, passports, licences, taxes, scholarships, pensions, health and education services, grievance redressal, DigiLocker, UMANG and CSCs. G2G (Government to Government): e-Office, PFMS, CCTNS and ICJS, e-Courts, GSTN, data sharing and monitoring dashboards - improving internal coordination. G2B (Government to Business): MCA21, GST, customs (ICEGATE), single-window clearances, e-procurement (GeM), Udyam and PARIVESH - improving ease of doing business and transparency.

G2E (Government to Employee): e-HRMS, PFMS payroll, Bhavishya and Jeevan Pramaan for pensions, SPARROW appraisals, iGOT Karmayogi training and biometric attendance - improving personnel management. Some scholars also identify C2G (citizen to government - feedback, petitions, participation via MyGov) and G2N (government to non-profit organisations - NGO Darpan portal).

Significance: these models show that digital government affects both internal administration (G2G, G2E) and external relationships (G2C, G2B). An integrated approach - with common platforms (India Stack), interoperability and citizen-centric design - is necessary to realise the full benefits of e-governance.

sections.title: E-Administration, Service Delivery and Good Governance

blocks.text:
E-administration uses digital tools for internal processes such as records, communication and workflow. E-service delivery uses digital channels to provide services to the public.

Digital systems can support transparency and accountability by improving access to information and creating traceable administrative processes. Their value depends on whether technology actually improves citizen-oriented governance rather than merely shifting old procedures online.

E-administration: digital internal processes - e-Office files, digital signatures, workflow automation, financial and HR systems, video conferencing and dashboards; benefits - speed, reduced paperwork, audit trails and coordination; challenges - training, work culture, security and the risk of digitising red tape. E-service delivery: online and mobile services, CSCs, digital payments, DBT using the JAM trinity, and time-bound service delivery; benefits - convenience, speed, lower costs and reduced corruption; challenges - digital divide, authentication failures and the need for assisted access.

Transparency and accountability: proactive disclosure, open data, online tracking, e-procurement, dashboards, social audit support and geo-tagging improve transparency; audit trails, grievance redressal, time-bound services, feedback and reduced discretion improve accountability.

Good governance: e-governance can promote participation, rule of law, transparency, responsiveness, equity, effectiveness and accountability (World Bank and UNDP criteria). However, its value depends on whether technology actually improves citizen-oriented governance - through process re-engineering, inclusion, security, privacy protection and institutional accountability - rather than merely shifting old procedures online. The Second ARC's recommendations and Digital India's vision emphasise this citizen-centric approach.

sections.title: Challenges: Digital Divide, Cybersecurity and Privacy

blocks.text:
E-governance faces important challenges. The digital divide can exclude people who lack connectivity, devices or digital skills. Cybersecurity threats can disrupt systems or compromise data, while privacy requires responsible handling of personal information.

Other challenges include infrastructure, interoperability, administrative capacity and resistance to change. Successful e-governance therefore requires secure technology, accessible services and capable institutions.

Digital divide: unequal access to devices, connectivity and digital skills by income, location, gender, age, education, disability and language; causes exclusion from services and benefits; measures - BharatNet, PM-WANI, CSCs, PMGDISHA digital literacy, regional language services (Bhashini), accessibility standards and offline alternatives. Cybersecurity: threats such as hacking, ransomware (AIIMS 2022), phishing, data breaches and attacks on critical infrastructure; framework - IT Act (2000/2008), CERT-In, NCIIPC, National Cyber Security Policy (2013), I4C and the 1930 helpline; measures - security audits, encryption, authentication, backups and training.

Privacy: large-scale data collection raises concerns of surveillance and misuse; Puttaswamy (2017) recognised privacy as a fundamental right; the Aadhaar judgement (2018) limited mandatory use; the Digital Personal Data Protection Act (2023) and Rules (2025) provide consent-based processing, rights of data principals, duties of data fiduciaries, a Data Protection Board and penalties, though government exemptions are criticised.

Other challenges and solutions: infrastructure gaps, interoperability, resistance to change, lack of skilled personnel, costs, process re-engineering and vendor dependence. Successful e-governance requires secure technology, inclusive and accessible services, privacy safeguards, trained and motivated personnel, institutional capacity and citizen participation. In Mizoram, overcoming connectivity challenges in hilly terrain and building digital literacy are key priorities.
